1: Let us first consider what Micah signifies in Latin. It means 'Who is from God' or as we find elsewhere 'who is this man,' the son of the Morasthite, that is, the heir? Now, who is this heir, but the Son of God, Who says, All things are given unto Me of My Father; and Who, being Himself the Heir, would have us His co-heirs. And well may we say 'Who is that man?' not one of the people, but chosen to receive the grace of God, in whom the Holy Spirit speaks, who began to prophesy in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah kings of Judah. By which order is signified the course of the vision, for the progress is from the times of evil kings to that of a good king.

Micah, on whom I now desire to dictate commentaries, is third in the order of the twelve prophets according to the Seventy translators, sixth according to the Hebrew truth; and he follows the prophet Jonah, who succeeds Obadiah, and so it comes about that Amos is third, and Joel second after Hosea, who is first among all. Therefore, placed as it were in the heart of the volume, he must contain deep mysteries; and the word of God, which always descends to the prophets, descends to Micah as well, which means humility; to Micah of Moresheth, which to this day is a rather small village near Eleutheropolis, a city of Palestine. Moresheth, moreover, in our language means heir. Beautifully, therefore, humility, which is even the foremost among the virtues, is born of the hope of the Lord's inheritance. But humility not of the kind that comes from the consciousness of sins, but that which is placed among the virtues, according to which it is said: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation, and: He who humbles himself shall be exalted, and: Before destruction the heart of a man is lifted up, and before glory it is humbled. Hence the Lord too: Learn, he says, from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. Just as, therefore, among us names of good wish, and as it were for an omen of virtue, are given, for example: Victor, Castus, Pius, Probus, and among the Greeks one is called σώφρων (temperate) and εὐσεβὴς (pious), and common nouns are turned into proper names, so among the Hebrews Micah too, and Obadiah and Zechariah and the others like them, are given to children by their parents from the name of a virtue.

The word of the Lord which came to Micah of Moresheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah: which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. Or according to the Seventy: Concerning the things which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. The word of the Lord, then, came to Micah after Hosea, Amos and Isaiah, who prophesied under Uzziah. From this we understand that Micah did not prophesy in the times of Uzziah, but in those of his son Jotham, after whom Ahaz reigned, Hezekiah succeeding to the rule of his father Ahaz, under whom the ten tribes were led into captivity by the Assyrians. As far, therefore, as concerns the history, according to the order of the captivity — because first Samaria, the metropolis of Israel, was taken, afterwards Jerusalem, the city of Judah —, the title of the prophecy is set down first concerning Samaria, second concerning Jerusalem. But as far as concerns the mystical understandings, since Samaria is always taken for heresies and Jerusalem for the Church, we say that the word of the Lord comes to Jerusalem and to the coheir of Christ, concerning perverse doctrines, and concerning the Church, if perhaps she has committed any sins, and that it weaves together the order of the whole volume. That Samaria, moreover, and the ten tribes, which were cut off from the stock of David under King Jeroboam, are taken in the person of the heretics, the whole of Scripture indeed bears witness, but above all the prophet Hosea, and this very book, which calls the heretics impious and the churchmen sinners. For it immediately follows: What is the impiety of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the sin of the house of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem? This, at least, according to the Seventy translators. How it is read in the Hebrew, however, we shall add a little later. But this too, that the heretics always trust in the supposed loftiness of their doctrines and despise the simplicity of the Church, is said in another place: Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria; for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. Moreover, Samaria fashioned for herself golden calves out of her own understanding, which had beauty indeed on the surface, but did not have the vital spirit, and she fashioned them in the house of God, which is the meaning of Bethel. For the people of Israel could not accept gods except those that were fashioned out of the Scriptures and in the house of God. But although they call their conventicles Bethel, yet after the fashioning of the idols it ceased to be Bethel, and is called Beth-aven, which means the house of the idol, for which the Seventy translated the house of Ὡν (On). So much for the title; now let us come to the opening of the prophecy, and, while the Lernaean beast rages, let us invoke the coming of the Holy Spirit. You, O Paula and Eustochium, pour out prayers to the Lord the Savior, that envy may not harm me, but that my mind, free, may think only of what it strives to explain, and may not feel the slaps of insults, which the Lord despised in his passion.

[Passage quoted, Micah i. 2-5.]

HERE, too, in this passage the Descent of the Lord coming forth from His place is proclaimed plainly. This must mean the Word of God, Whom I have proved in the previous books to be alone God and Lord after the Supreme and Almighty God. His place you would rightly understand to be the kingdom of heaven, and the glorious throne of His Divinity, of which the prophet sang in praise of God, saying, "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever,'' on which the Father bade Him sit as being His Only-begotten Son, saying, "Sit thou on my right hand." For I have already shewn that these words can only be referred to our Saviour, God the Word. So, then, the prophecy before us says that He comes forth from His place, and will descend upon the high-places of the earth. How are we to understand this? Shall we take it literally of the hills and mountains of Israel, which are the subjects of so many prophecies, Jerusalem itself and Mount Sion, in which our Lord and Saviour spent so much time? If so, their destruction and ruin at the descent of Christ would be prophesied. And it is the fact that after the Saviour's coming and the treatment He received all the hills mentioned were besieged, and utterly desolated. But the rulers of the Jewish people as well, and their kingdom that existed previously, their sacrificial system and the seats of their teachers, here called Mountains metaphorically, are said to be shaken by the Descent of the Lord from heaven. And who could deny that this was fulfilled after the time of our Saviour Jesus Christ, when he sees all these things not only shaken, but abolished? And the valleys even now melting are the Jewish synagogues established in all cities instead of Jerusalem and Mount Sion, which are full of lamentation and wailing, and melting as wax at the fire with grief and extreme sorrow for the desolation of their homes and their long and lasting slavery. And the coming of the Word of God regarded in another light took place not in chasms and valleys, nor in lowly and earth-bound thoughts, but in exalted souls. And so the Lord Himself is said in a wider metaphor to be about to descend on the high-places of earth. Then the mountains shaken under Him will be those very heights whither He "was led by the spirit to be tempted of the devil," "when the devil leadeth him to an exceeding high mountain, and he was with the wild beasts." Or the mountains again might represent in metaphor the idolatry practised formerly on mountains, and the principalities and powers working there invisibly, which our Saviour's teaching was to shake and overthrow in no small degree. For His inspired word and His miraculous and wondrous strength have insensibly destroyed the powers which from far ages have attacked mankind. In like manner also the hills melting like wax from the presence of the fire would be the infernal and earth-bound daemons, against whom He sent forth fire to consume their lust, saying, "I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what will I if it be already kindled?" Burned by which fire, and unable to bear the torture of its unseen flame, they withdrew from the bodies of men, and acknowledged that which controlled them and drove them out, crying, "Let us alone, what have we to do with thee, Son of God? Hast thou come to torment us before the time? We know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God." And these He chiefly chastised, and destroyed their princes, because not content with the corruption of the other nations, whereby they had cast them all into the errors of polytheism, they had also plotted against God's ancient people, those of the Circumcision, and had endeavoured to seduce even them from their God to all manner of impiety. And this was the chief reason why the Lord descended from heaven. Wherefore He says next, "For the iniquity of Jacob is all this done, and for the transgression of my people Israel." And then He gives an additional reason for the Descent of the Word, recounting the impiety of the Jews, and the destruction falling upon them, and heralding the calling of all nations throughout the world. For these things' sake the Word of God came down from heaven to earth. Hear this passage:

"5. For the impiety of the House of Jacob is all this done, and for the transgression of the House of Israel. What is the impiety of the House of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the sin of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem? 6. And I will make Samaria a lodge of the field, and a plantation of a vineyard, and I will draw down to chaos the stones thereof, and will hide the foundations thereof."

And He adds:

"12. Evil hath descended from the Lord on the gates of Jerusalem, the noise of chariots and horsemen."

And again:

"15. O glory of the daughter of Jerusalem, shave and cut off thy choice children. Enlarge thy widowhood, as an eagle, when thy captives are led from thee."

And moreover:

"Sion shall be ploughed as a field, and Jerusalem shall be as a granary, and the mount of the house as a grove of the wood."

Sion and Jerusalem and the so-called "mount of the house" are what were represented before in, "And the mountains shall be shaken from beneath him, and the valleys shall be melted as wax before the fire for the iniquity of Jacob." For the mountains and the dwellers thereon were besieged for the iniquity they had wrought against Him soon and not long after Mount Sion was burned and left utterly desolate, and the Mount of the House of God became as a grove of the wood.

If our own observation has any value, we have seen in our own time Sion once so famous ploughed with yokes of oxen by the Romans and utterly devastated, and Jerusalem, as the oracle says, deserted like a lodge. And this has come to pass precisely because of their impieties, for the sake of which the Heavenly Word has come forth from His own place.

And I have already said that the Word of God came down from heaven and descended on the high places of the earth for other reasons, both that the mountains which of old lifted themselves up and exalted themselves against the knowledge of God might be shaken beneath Him (that is to say the opposing powers, which before His coming enslaved the Hebrew race as well as the rest of mankind in the practice of impiety and idolatry), and also that the evil daemons called valleys (through their living in gloomy chasms, and in the recesses of the body) might melt as wax before the fire and flee away from men by the power of the divine Word. And there was another additional reason by no means fortuitous for the descent of the Lord from heaven, which this prophecy recognizes, namely that all the nations on earth, the daemons being banished and the ruling spirits shaken, recovering from the cruel and ceaseless tyranny which had long afflicted them, might attain the knowledge of Almighty God. And the voice of the same prophet proclaims the same things further on as follows, uniting them in the same manner under one head:

"And in the last days the Mount of the Lord shall be glorious, prepared upon the tops of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills, and peoples shall haste unto it, and many nations shall come and say, Come, let us go up to the Mount of the Lord, and the house of the God of Jacob, and they will shew us his way, and we will walk in his paths. For out of Sion shall come forth a law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he will judge in the midst of the nations."

One can learn at one's leisure in what sense such prophecies of the Call of the Gentiles are to be understood, and that they were only fulfilled after the coming of our Saviour. And the opening of the prophecy is in full agreement with the truth that the Lord descended not only for the salvation of the Jewish race, but for that of all nations, in proclaiming to all peoples and all the inhabitants of the earth, saying, "Hear all peoples, and let the earth attend, and all that are therein." And it darkly foretold the witness of the Passion of our Lord, adding, "And the Lord our God shall be for a witness."

Hear, all you peoples, and let the earth attend, and its fullness, and let the Lord God be a witness to you, the Lord from his holy temple. LXX: Hear, all you peoples, and let the earth listen, and all who are in it, and let the Lord God be for a testimony to you: the Lord from his holy house. Since according to the history the sense is plain, I leave the understanding of it to the prudence of the reader. According to tropology, however, he calls together the peoples to hear, that is, the churches of the whole world, and the earth to listen, because the earthly doctrines of the heretics have been built up in it. That heresies, moreover, are numbered among the works of the flesh, which is always referred to the earth, the Apostle does not pass over in silence in writing to the Galatians, and the Lord in the Gospel shows to the prudent hearer: He who is of the earth speaks of the earth. And to distinguish them, he says again of the churchmen: But he who comes from heaven is above all, and: What he has seen and heard, to this he bears witness. If, however, what he says, Hear, you peoples, because of that saying of the Lord, He who has ears to hear, let him hear, sounds something more than what is brought in afterwards, Let the earth attend, we shall apply to the Church: Hear, all you peoples. But to the heretics, who have taken up an earthly doctrine: Let the earth attend, and all who are in it, so that, if these hear and those attend, they may not suffer the things which the word of the Lord afterwards threatens. And let the Lord be for a testimony to them, or, as it is read in the Hebrew, for a witness, or, as Symmachus more plainly translated it, testifying, and testifying from nowhere else than from his own house, which is the Church, or surely in the Son, that is, in our Lord Jesus Christ, who is truly the temple of God the Father, and from whose mouth the Father speaks, piercing the inward parts and the marrow of those who are willing to attend and to hear.

Now let us also consider Jesus' statement, "I have proceeded and come from God." It seems useful to me to juxtapose to these words the following words from Micah: "Hear my words, you people, and let the earth and all who are in it pay attention; and the Lord shall be among you for a witness, the Lord from his holy house. Therefore behold, the Lord proceeds from his place and will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains will be shaken under him, and the valleys will be dissolved like wax, before fire and like water tumbling down in a waterfall." Now consider whether the statement, "I have proceeded from God," is equivalent to the statement, "The Lord proceeds from his place," since, when the Son is in the Father, being in the form of God before he empties himself, God is his place, as it were.… Unless you understand that the Son is in the Father in a different way than he was before he proceeded from God, it will seem contradictory that he has both proceeded from God, and, after he has proceeded from God, is still in God.

"I have come down," he says, "that I may see." When responses are conveyed to Abraham, God is not said to come down, but to stand over him, as we expounded above: "three men stood," it says, "over him." But now, because the cause of sinners is being dealt with, God is said to come down. See that you do not perceive an ascent and descent of place. For frequently this is found in the divine letters, as in the prophet Micah: "behold," he says, "the Lord has gone out from his holy place and has come down and will tread upon the high places of the earth." God therefore is said to come down, when he deigns to have care of human frailty. Which is to be understood more especially of our Lord and Savior, who "did not deem it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." He came down therefore. "For no one else has ascended into heaven, except him who came down from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven." For the Lord came down not only to care for, but also to bear, the things which are ours. "For he took the form of a servant," and although he himself is of invisible nature, as being equal to the Father, yet he took a visible appearance, "and was found in appearance as a man."

I HAVE already considered this prophecy among the passages. And I have pointed out that only from the date of our Saviour Jesus Christ's Coming among men have the objects of Jewish reverence, the hill called Zion and Jerusalem, the buildings there, that is to say, the Temple, the Holy of Holies, the Altar, and whatever else was there dedicated to the glory of God, been utterly removed or shaken, in fulfilment of the Word which said:

"Behold the Lord, the Lord comes forth from his place, and he shall descend on the high places of the earth, and the mountains shall be shaken under him."

And when those kings are shaken, the souls of the Jews, called "valleys," because of the contrast of their wretchedness with their former exaltation, bewailing the passing of the aforesaid glory, will melt like wax before the fire, and be as water rushing down a chasm, through the multitude of those that fall from bad to worse. And all this it says will come to pass because of the sin of the house of Jacob, and the transgression of the house of Israel.

and the place of the Lord is every one in whom he finds lodging, or certainly the Son is the place of the Father, just as the Father too is the place of the Son, as the Lord Savior says: I in the Father, and the Father in me; Micah too signifies this same thing: Behold, the Lord will go forth from his place, and will come down upon the high places of the earth; and the mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before the fire, and like water that is carried down a steep place: for when the Lord Savior came down and set out from the Father, the high places of the earth and the mountains were shaken, and the lower parts of the valleys were melted;

Tropologically, however, the Lord will go forth from his place, by which we can understand either the Son or all the saints. For the Son himself says: I am in the Father, and the Father in me, and of the saints: I will dwell and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. From these, then, he will go forth, not that he abandons them; for the word of the Lord also went forth from the apostles to those who heard, and yet it did not leave them; and places of this kind, that is, those which deserve to have God as their guest, rising as it were with Christ and sitting with him in the heavenly places, are set on high. Hence too he is said to come down to those who cannot hear his teaching on the mountain. And when he has come down, he will not go up upon the lowly and upon those who are placed below, but upon those who are called the high places of the earth, and who, understanding the majesty of the Lord as he comes, will be shaken. And although they are mountains, yet they will tremble at the presence of such a charioteer or rider. But the valleys, that is, souls set into χοϊκοῖς (earthy) bodies and not rising with the heavenly man, will not be able to bear his presence, but whatever is hard in them will be dissolved, and so they will flow, as if waters had no level ground and were borne headlong into the depth.

For behold, the Lord will go forth from his place, and he will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains will be consumed beneath him, and the valleys will be split like wax before the fire, like waters that run down headlong; for the crime of Jacob is all this, and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the crime of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what are the high places of Judah? Are they not Jerusalem? LXX: For behold, the Lord will go forth from his place, and will come down, and will go up upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before the fire, and like water flowing down a slope; because of the impiety of Jacob are all these things, and because of the sin of the house of Israel. What is the impiety of the house of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the sin of the house of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem? O Samaria and Jerusalem, hear, and diligently attend to the Lord testifying to you from his temple and foretelling whatever he is going to do. Behold, the Lord will go forth from his place. For he who is meek and kind, and whose nature is clemency, is compelled for your sake to take on the character of cruelty, which he does not have. And he will come down and tread upon the high places of the earth. The descent of God, and the running down of his majesty to lower things, is to tread the earth and to crush all the powerful. The mountains, he says, will be consumed, or will melt, and the valleys beneath him, by which we are to understand princes and peoples. And just as wax does not endure the nearness of fire, and waters are borne headlong in a downward course, so all the pride of the impious, when the Lord comes, will be dissolved and will flow away. All this, moreover, will happen because of the crimes of the ten tribes, which he calls Jacob and Israel, and because of the transgression of Judah, since among the ten tribes Samaria was the metropolis, and in the kingdom of Judah Jerusalem fashioned the idols of the high places; this according to the letter.

It can also be understood thus: that because of the impieties of Samaria and the crimes of the Jews the Lord went forth from what was once his place, and said to the Jews: Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate. And he came down from the heavens, and went up upon the high places of the earth, that is, upon those who, believing out of the lowliness of the Gentiles, deserved to be lofty. And the mountains were shaken, the doctrines of the philosophers and lofty kingdoms, and those who remained lowly were consumed and crushed by the coming of the Savior; and as the Church grew and the mountains rose on high, the idols fell down into the depth. The Lord, therefore, went forth from his place, and the Church was built from the Gentiles, so that the mountains might be moved beneath his feet and the depths of the valleys dissolved, because Jacob acted impiously, and Israel sinned, and all the tribes denied the Lord.

On another occasion when he was sitting by himself some place reading the book of the twelve prophets, he came to the prophet Micah. An angel of the Lord appeared to him and asked him about this verse from Micah: "Like water coming down from its source." He said to him, "What do you think it means?" While he was still puzzling over it, trying to understand, the angel answered, "Theodore, why do you not perceive its meaning? Is it not obvious that it is the water of the river coming down from paradise?" As soon as the angel had said this, he ceased to see him.

The Lord, therefore, will come, terrible for teaching, that is, for moving the mountains and for dissolving the lowness of the valleys, because Jacob committed impiety, and Israel sin. But the impiety of Jacob is the conventicles of the heretics, which are called Samaria. And the sin of Judah, that is, of him who confesses the Lord, is nothing other than Jerusalem, in which many crimes are found. That the house of Judah, moreover, is referred to Christ, whose Church it is, we have both often said, and let us set down this for the present: Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the back of your enemies.

But since we have once understood Samaria as the church of the heretics, which, separated from God, has become a conventicle of the people, the Lord himself threatens that he will make her a watch-hut for fruit, a field and a planting of a vineyard. For it is much better that a useless city be overthrown, and the stones with which it had been built be pulled down headlong, and that it be prepared for an orchard and a planting of vineyards, than that it remain in a most wicked building. For when her foundations have been destroyed and laid bare, — those by which she seemed to conceal her mysteries and to have firm doctrines on which she stood; and when all the idols which seemed to have outward show, and a beauty composed by artful speech, have been cut to pieces by the ministers of God, that is, by churchmen —, then in the place of the most wicked building the various fruits of the Church will spring up, and not only will they spring up, but they will also be guarded, and the vine of Sorek will be planted, from which may come the wine which the Lord promised that he would drink in the kingdom of the Father. And not only will her foundations, which before were pressed down by earth, be opened and brought out into the open, and the idols which she had fashioned for herself be cut to pieces, but the glory too and the riches which she seemed to have from her fornication and her error will be consumed by my fire, of which I said in the Gospel: I came to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it may burn, and they will be burned up and reduced to nothing, because they were not acquired from the truth of doctrines, but from the fornication of the soul, and were collected from error here and there. For the heretics do not have riches coming from a paternal inheritance, but every day they find something to worship, and fashion idols for themselves with an artful hand and a curious mind.

And I will make Samaria like a heap of stones in the field when a vineyard is planted, and I will pull down her stones into the valley, and I will lay bare her foundations, and all her carved images shall be cut to pieces, and all her wages shall be burned with fire, and all her idols I will lay waste; for they were gathered from the wages of a harlot, and to the wages of a harlot they shall return. For this I will lament and howl, I will go stripped and naked, I will make a lamentation like that of the dragons, and a mourning like that of the ostriches, for her wound is desperate, for it has come even to Judah, and has touched the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem. LXX: And I will make Samaria a watch-hut for fruit in the field, and a planting of a vineyard; and I will pull down her stones into the abyss, and I will lay bare her foundations, and all her carved images shall fall to pieces, and all her wages they shall burn with fire, and all her idols I will lay waste, for from the wages of fornication she gathered, and from the wages of fornication she destroyed. Because of this she shall lament and mourn, she shall go barefoot and naked, she shall make a lamentation like that of the dragons, and a mourning like that of the daughters of the Sirens; for her wound has prevailed, for it has come even to Judah, and has touched even to the gate of my people, even into Jerusalem. According to the order of the sins comes the order of the punishments. Samaria sinned first, and fashioned idols, and worshipped calves in place of the Lord; let her therefore also be the first to perish. I will destroy her when the Assyrians come, and I will make her like a heap of stones when a vineyard is planted, so that she is reduced to mounds. And I will pull down her stones into the valley. For she was situated in the mountains, where Sebaste now is, in which the bones of Saint John the Baptist are also laid to rest. And I will lay bare her foundations. For so great will the ruin be, and so great the overthrow of the city, that not only will the walls and buildings fall, but the foundations too will be laid bare down to the last stone.

And all her carved images, and all the riches that various kings had brought together into her, will be cut to pieces and burned with fire and reduced to nothing. For the wealth and the manifold furnishings, which had been gathered, as was thought, from the fornication of idols, will be carried off to another harlot, that is, to Nineveh, so that, just as in their own land they committed fornication with the idols which they made, so they may go to another land of idols and of fornication, that is, to the Assyrians. Thus far concerning Samaria.

And since the same wound is to reach Jerusalem — for she too sinned with a like error, forsaking her God and fashioning idols —, for that reason the prophet makes as it were a προσωποποιίαν (personification) of God, and under his own person brings in the feeling of one who laments, and says: For this I will lament and howl, I will go stripped and naked; for I have lost the ten tribes, and I will make a lamentation like that of the dragons, and a mourning like that of the ostriches. For just as dragons resound with a terrible hissing, according to the accounts of those who have written on natural things, at the time when they are overcome by elephants, and as ostriches are forgetful of their eggs and, as though they had not given birth, leave their young in the sand to be trampled by the feet of beasts, of which it is written more fully in Job, so I too shall go about without children, stripped and naked. And I will do this because her wound is desperate, that is, Samaria's. And the same sin, or rather the same punishment of sin, which had overthrown Samaria, will come even to Judah and even to the gate of my city Jerusalem. For as Samaria was overthrown by the Assyrians, so Judah and Jerusalem will be overthrown by the Chaldeans.

Because of this, when their field has been turned into a watch-hut for fruit and prepared for vineyards, and the stones with which the city had been built have been pulled down into the depth, and their foundations have been laid bare, and all the carved images cut to pieces and burned, and the wages which they promised themselves with vain hope, and whatever they seemed to worship as God, reduced to nothing, because they had procured every reward for themselves from the fornication of the soul, then, understanding their former error and returning to themselves, they will lament over the things at which they used to laugh, and they will mourn over the things in which, committing fornication, they formerly in some way rejoiced. And they will put off from their feet whatever deadly thing they had, and they will be barefoot, because the ground on which they are to stand is a holy place, and they will cast away all the garments of their fornication; and they will be naked, so that they may be clothed with the garment of Christ, and they will make a lamentation like that of the dragons. For the dragons too will one day lament, when they see the greatest dragon captured and hanging on the fisherman's hook, and the sea made desolate. And they will mourn like the daughters of the Sirens, for the songs of the heretics are sweet, and deceive the peoples with a pleasant voice. Nor can anyone pass by their songs unless he has stopped his ear and escaped as if deaf.

And this Samaria of such a kind will lament and mourn for this reason: because, wounded by the arrow of the Lord and receiving the wound of the word, she will recognize her error. And not only did she herself sin, but she also wished to bring her iniquity and her error into the gates of Judah. Hence it is said of her: It has come even to Judah, and has touched even to the gates of my people, even to Jerusalem. She touched the gates, he says, by which we understand the ears. But she could not enter the middle of the city; for if she had entered, she would have made Jerusalem a Samaria. Whenever we see some in the Church scandalized at the discourses of the heretics, and asking how to answer their questions, and yet not withdrawing from the Church, let us say: Samaria, or the wound of Samaria, has come even to the confessing people, even to the ears of the people of God, and even to the ears of Jerusalem. For what is said, it has touched even to the gates of my people, is to be understood ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (in common), so that this is understood as well: it has touched even to the gates of Jerusalem. Thus far against Samaria and against Jerusalem; let us look also at the rest that follows.

In Gath do not announce it, do not weep with tears; in the house of dust sprinkle yourselves with dust; pass over for yourselves, dwelling of Shaphir, confounded with shame; she who dwells in Zaanan has not gone out. The house of Ezel will receive mourning from you, the house that stood by itself, for she who dwells in Maroth has grown weak unto good; for evil has come down from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem. The tumult of the chariot of astonishment for the one dwelling in Lachish is the beginning of sin for the daughter of Zion, for in you were found the crimes of Israel. Therefore he will give emissaries upon the inheritance of Gath; the house of lying, for a deception to the kings of Israel. Still I will bring an heir to you who dwell in Mareshah; the glory of Israel will come as far as Adullam. LXX: You who are in Gath, do not be magnified; you who are in Bachim, do not build out of a house of mockeries; sprinkle earth on your derision, you who inhabit its cities well; the inhabitress of Zaanan has not gone out. Mourn for the house next to her; she will receive from you a blow of pain, who began unto good, she who dwells in pains? For evils have come down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem. The sound of chariots and horsemen, the dwelling of Lachish, is the chief of sin to the daughter of Zion, for in you were found the iniquities of Israel. Therefore he will give emissaries as far as the inheritance of Gath; vain houses, they were in vain to the kings of Israel, until I bring heirs to you, you who dwell in Lachish; the inheritance will come as far as Adullam. The Hebrew disagrees greatly with the translation of the LXX, and both my translation and theirs are wrapped in such great difficulties that, if ever we have needed the Spirit of God, and indeed in expounding his holy Scriptures we always need his coming, now most of all we long for him to be present, and to unfold what he spoke in the prophets, so that what he himself deigns to promise elsewhere may be understood of us too: Open your mouth, and I will fill it. Gath, as the history of Kingdoms also testifies, is one of the five cities of Philistia, near the border of Judea, and for those going from Eleutheropolis to Gaza it is even now a very large village; from there too came that Goliath of Gath whom David killed in battle. Since, therefore, the prophet, or rather the Lord through the prophet, had said: I will mourn and howl, I will go despoiled and naked; I will make a lamentation like that of dragons, and mourning like that of ostriches, for the wound of Samaria is desperate and incurable, and it has come even to Judah and has touched the gate of my people, Jerusalem, for this reason I still command with the voice of one weeping: Do not announce it in Gath, lest the enemies hear and rejoice; do not weep with tears, that is, let not even your grief burst out into sobs; hide your weeping, lest your adversaries exult; let your faces have no tears, though your breast have grief; do not go outside, but in the house of dust sprinkle yourselves with the crumbling ash of the ruins.

Gath means winepress; those, therefore, who are in Gath, that is, in the winepress, thinking that they have gathered the vintage of the fruit of life and trodden the cluster from the vine of Sorek, are lifted up into pride, not knowing that the cluster of the land of Judea is not found in the territories of the Philistines. Do not, he says, be lifted up, you who are in the winepresses. For your vine is of the vine of Sodom, and your shoot of Gomorrah, and your grape is of bitterness, and you have a cluster of gall, and the fury of dragons is your wine, the incurable fury of asps. For even if you should bear fruit — since your vintage is not only of Sodom and Gomorrah, but also of Egypt and the other hostile nations —, the Lord will give your fruit to the blight, and your labors to the locust, and will kill your vineyards with hail, and your mulberry trees with frost. Let not the likeness of wine deceive you, and do not call the bitter sweet; taste your wine more carefully, and you will find, in place of the wine of Sorek, the fury of dragons and the venom of asps. Therefore do not be proud, but rather humble yourselves under the mighty hand of the Lord, and pass over to that winepress of which he who comes up from Edom, and ruddy from Bozrah, speaks in Isaiah the prophet: I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there is no man with me. Again, since there are others too of foreign race, for the province of the Philistines has many regions and cities, who through evil works and thoughts contrary to God say: We have been destroyed, but let us return and build up what has been destroyed. Hence they are also called the borders of impiety, and the people with whom the Lord is angry. To them it is said: You who are in Bachim, do not build from a house of mockeries. Bachim in our language signifies mourning and weeping. In short, except for the Seventy, all translated κλαυθμὸν, that is, weeping. You, therefore, who are engaged in works and opinions of this kind, which are worthy of weeping, do not renew a most wicked building; and do not suppose your own understanding to be God's edifice, nor build upon sand, lest, when the storm comes and your house falls, the empty labor offer laughter to those who see it. Rather, understanding that your building is worthy of derision, sprinkle your heads with its ruins and dust, and repent, because you wished without counsel to build a house that would fall.

Pass over for yourselves, dwelling of Shaphir, which in the Syriac and Hebrew language means beautiful. For Samaria is shown even now, situated in the most beautiful and most fertile place of Judea. It is said to her, therefore: O you who dwell in a most fertile region, since you are confounded with shame, so pass over, so be led away into captivity, that because of the greatness of your evils not even your neighbor the Philistine may hear your voice. Moreover, what follows: She who dwells in Zaanan has not gone out, which means going out, or as Symmachus renders: The abundant dwelling has not gone out, is said of the same Samaria, which is at the very doors of the Assyrian captivity, and as soon as she is moved from her borders, enters hostile land. For the abundant dwelling is to be taken in the sense of what we have already said above, the beautiful dwelling. She, therefore, who dwelt in the going out, or in abundance, did not go out of her own will, but was led by force to the Assyrians. Hence the neighboring house, at the side, which is what Ezel means, namely the kingdom of Judah, will receive mourning from you, she who now for the time being, Samaria having been captured, stood firm and had God as her defender.

There follows: She who dwells well in her cities has not gone out, dwelling in Zaanan. This seems to me to have this meaning: You who are proud in Gath and in Bachim, in vain do you try to build a house worthy of laughter; sprinkle yourselves with dust and repent, because you wished to press out a detestable wine and to construct a building contrary to God. But the Church of Christ, which dwells well, and, possessing churches in the whole world, is joined by the unity of the Spirit, and has the cities of the law, of the prophets and of the Gospel, and of the apostles, has not gone out of her borders, that is, out of the holy Scriptures, but keeps the possession she entered upon, because she dwells in Zaanan, which Symmachus, as we said above, rendered abundance; for she has the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, with whom are all spiritual graces and abundance of virtues. Hence it is said to her: Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers. But you who dwell beside Zaanan, that is, beside the abundant Church, O you heretics, O contrary doctrines, mourn for yourselves, because you have built yourselves a house for derision, and have pressed the winepress into pride, and have built your house not in the Scriptures but in the neighborhood of the Scriptures, a house now worthy not of laughter but of mourning and tears. Hence it is also added: mourn for the house which is beside her, that is, beside Zaanan. But what is added, She will receive from you a blow of pain, is said to the same heretics who are commanded to mourn for the house neighboring the Church, because the enemy and avenger, the devil, to whom they are to be handed over for punishment, himself inflicts blows on them, and for their most wicked building wrings out of them the pain of the blows. These are inflicted for this reason, that, perceiving the sins they had committed, they may repent, and the dwelling of pains may be for them an occasion of good things. Or else the pain of the Church is indicated, because she mourns her one-time sons, and she herself is the cause of the heretics' salvation, if they are willing to return to their grieving mother.

And she received mourning, and was struck with fear and weakened in her good, she who dwells in Maroth, that is, in bitternesses; or as Symmachus renders: The dwelling provoking to bitterness, that is, ἡ κατοικία ἡ παραπικραίνουσα, which in Hebrew is called iosebeth maroth, on account of the captivity of the neighboring tribes, because evil came down from the Lord to the gate of Jerusalem; for the Assyrian, after laying waste Samaria, came also to Jerusalem, at the time when Rabshakeh was sent, hurling insults, about whom both the fourth book of Kingdoms (2 Kings) and Isaiah write more fully. There it is said that the Assyrian king sent from Lachish to Jerusalem, and afterwards, Lachish having been taken, passed on to attack Libnah.

Moreover, as to what is brought in, For evils have come down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem, the Marcionites and the Manichaeans too use this text, on the ground that the God of the law is the author of evils. Let us say that evils came down from the Lord in the way that the Savior also speaks in the Gospel: I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven. For as there Lucifer, who rose in the morning, fell from heaven and was crushed upon the earth, he who used to send to the nations, so also these evils, which fell from the Lord and came to the gates of Jerusalem, were not evils before they fell, but because they fell headlong from the Lord, for that reason they became evils. And that we may know the snares of the evils: They came, he says, to the gates of Jerusalem, which, because they are strong and adamantine, are shut by the apostles, to whom the keys of Jerusalem have been entrusted; before them the enemies roam about, and whomever they see going out, they kill. If anyone, therefore, is of Jerusalem, which dwells well in her cities, he does not go out, since he dwells in abundance; but he remains always within, and does not go out of her gates, for whoever goes out of them is killed; and he is killed by those who lift themselves up in Gath, and dwell in Bachim, and build a house for derision. In short, the evils which came down from the Lord to the gates of Jerusalem have only the din of chariots and the tumult of horses, and a confused sound before the doors of Jerusalem, so that with the lance of their mouth they may kill whomever they see wandering.

Therefore, O Lachish, city given over to idols, the chariot and cavalry of the Assyrians will come to you too, because in you also were found the crimes of Israel, and you were the beginning of idolatry in Judah; for through you, as through a gate, the impiety of the ten tribes migrated into Jerusalem.

After this it is written: You who dwell in Lachish: she is the chief of sin for the daughter of Zion. Lachish is interpreted πορεία ἐστὶν, that is, walking. And so these too, who went up in their chariots, and had horsemen, and only din and empty sound, to whom she who dwells well in her cities said, These in chariots and these on horses, but we will call upon the name of the Lord our God; because they moved their feet, and were carried about by every wind of false doctrine, and wished to go out from the Church, which is interpreted watchtower, that is, Zion, were the chiefs of sin for the daughter of Zion. And in her, that is, in Lachish, were found the impieties of Israel, which separated the people of God from its former kingdom. She, then, who dwells in Lachish, that is, in a most evil walking, with a step ever wavering, is the chief of sin for the daughter of Zion; and the impiety of Israel is in those who always move their feet and are said to dwell in Lachish.

And not only upon Lachish will the tumult and the chariots come, but also upon Gath, the chief city of Philistia, of which I had said above: In Gath do not announce it; for the Assyrian will send his brigands, whom he calls emissaries, and will possess the house of idolatry and the city of lying, which was a stumbling to the kings of Israel. As for what follows: Still I will bring an heir to you who dwell in Mareshah, he has alluded beautifully to the name; for since Mareshah means inheritance, he called the coming of the enemies into her heirs; and Mareshah, that is, the inheritance, will come as far as Adullam, a city of Judah, which Adullam is glorious among the cities of Israel. In short, Symmachus too translated thus: Ἔτι κληρονόμον ἄξω καί σοι κατοικία Μαρέσα, ἕως Ὀδολλὰμ ἥξει τῆς δόξης Ισραὴλ, that is: Still I will bring an heir to you too, dwelling of Mareshah; as far as Adullam will come of the glory of Israel; that is, you who are glorious among the cities of Israel. And where gloriae is said, let it be the genitive case of the singular number, huius gloriae, of this glory, and not the nominative plural, hae gloriae, these glories. Or certainly let us understand it thus: The captivity of Israel which came to Lachish, and Gath, and Mareshah, will come as far as Adullam too. And of the glory of Israel should be read more pointedly, so that κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν (by antiphrasis) ignominy or devastation is meant. Moreover, as to our having interpreted above the city of the prophet, Moresheth, as inheritance, let the reader know that in the same little verse which we set down, Therefore he will give emissaries upon the inheritance of Gath, in the Hebrew, maraseth Geth is written for the inheritance of Gath. Thus far, according to the Hebrew, as best we could and as it seemed to us, certainly as we heard it from the Hebrews, we have steered our little boat as though among rocks and very sharp crags; whether it has entered port or still tosses on the open sea, it will be for the reader's prudence to judge. Now, by your prayers, let us go on to other waves, and, with shipwreck of the exposition threatening on this side and on that, let us escape if we can.

Emissaries too will be given as far as the inheritance of Gath: Gath most wicked, and a winepress of poisons, which is built against the house of God, where there are vain houses, which were built for derision. And these vain houses were made in vain for the kings of Israel: as far as the history is concerned, for those kings whose sins are written in the books of Kingdoms and of Chronicles; but as far as anagogy is concerned, for the chiefs of the heretics and the leaders of perverse doctrines; for to them the houses are vain and built in vain. And they last only so long, until the heirs who are to be brought in by the Lord hold them.

After this there follows: You who dwell in Lachish, the inheritance will come as far as Adullam. Adullam means testimony of the draught, or of their drawing, which in Greek is expressed more significantly, μαρτυρία ἀντλήσεως αὐτῶν. We read in Proverbs: If you are evil, you alone will draw up evils. She, therefore, who dwells in Lachish, that is, on a most evil road, will come to the testimony of her own draining, which she will drain and drink down according to the measure of her works. Or certainly it should be punctuated so that what is said, you who dwell in Lachish, is referred to what precedes, and the order and sense is: I will bring heirs to you from the Church, you who dwell in Lachish, because you too will be of the inheritance of the Lord, when you have drained and received what you deserve. At the end of this section I beseech the reader not to take necessity for choice, nor to judge a lengthy exposition to be verbosity, and to marvel rather that in places so rough I find anything at all, than that I leave out none of the things that have to be said.

Make yourself bald and be shorn over the sons of your delights; enlarge your baldness like the eagle, for they have been led captive from you. LXX: Glory of the daughter of Israel, make yourself bald and be shorn over your delicate sons; enlarge your baldness like the eagle, for they have been led captive from you. What was said by the Seventy, glory of the daughter of Israel, with their addition of the daughter, the Hebrews read at the end of the preceding section. But since you wished it so, and we have once undertaken it, the necessity lies upon us of interpreting the Scriptures as they are read in the Church, and nonetheless of not omitting the Hebrew truth. It is said, then, to Israel, for the present according to the letter, so that we take either the ten tribes in Samaria, or all Israel in common, that, since the people has been led captive and all Judea laid waste by the Assyrians and the Babylonians, they should take up mourning and weep for their sons. And as the eagle, which is the queen of birds, at a certain time loses its feathers and remains featherless, so let Israel too lay aside all its glory, with which it had formerly been surrounded, and mourn its sons, made subject to the power of enemies. That the eagle is accustomed to lose its plumage at a certain time is written both in the Psalter, Your old age will be renewed like the eagle's, and by the Comic poet in the Heautontimorumenos: She seemed, he says, truly, as the saying goes, an eagle's old age. But if we wish to take this same thing also of the present time of the Jewish overthrow, we shall see that all the grace with which they once flourished before God has completely departed from them. For where is the prophet? Where is the teacher of the law? Where the protection of angels? Where the victory hoped for by the few against the many? Jerusalem has been made bald and has lost all the hair of her former glory, and her sons, who cried out against the Lord, Crucify, crucify him, have been led into captivity. I have read in someone's commentaries that what is said, Make yourself bald and be shorn over the sons of your delights, can be taken of the human condition, so that the speech of God is directed to Adam, or to the heavenly Jerusalem: O human soul, O city once mother of the saints, you who were formerly in paradise and enjoyed the delights of diverse trees, and had most beautiful hair, now, because you have been cast down from the heights and led away into Babylon, and have come into the place of captivity, and have lost your hair, shave yourself and put on the garb of a penitent; and you who formerly flew like an eagle on high, mourn your sons, mourn your offspring, which has been led captive out of you.

What happened to her we know was said through the prophet concerning Judea: Enlarge your baldness like the eagle. For the baldness of a man usually occurs only on the head, but the baldness of an eagle occurs over the whole body, because when it has grown very old, its feathers and plumes fall from all its limbs. Therefore she enlarges her baldness like an eagle, because she has lost her feathers, she who has lost her people. The feathers of her wings also fell, with which she was accustomed to fly to prey, because all her powerful men have perished, through whom she seized the things of others.
2: Woe to you who devise what is useless, and work evil on your beds; in the morning light they do it, for their hand is against God; and they coveted fields and took them by violence, and seized houses, and they wronged a man and his house, a man and his inheritance. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I devise evil against this family, from which you shall not withdraw your necks, and you shall not walk proudly, for it is a most evil time. In that day a parable shall be taken up over you, and a song shall be sung with sweetness by those who say: We have been laid waste with devastation; the portion of my people has been changed. How will it depart from me, when he returns who divides our lands? Because of this you will have no one casting the cord of the lot in the assembly of the Lord. LXX: They have become men who devise toils and work evils on their beds, and at once in the day they will accomplish them, because they did not lift up their hands to God; and they desired fields, and plundered orphans, and oppressed houses, and seized a man and his house, a man and his inheritance. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I devise evils against this tribe, from which you shall not withdraw your necks, that you may not walk upright suddenly, for it is a most evil time. In that day a parable shall be taken up over you, and a lament shall be lamented in a song of those who say: In misery we have been made miserable; the portion of my people has been measured out by the cord, and there was no one to forbid him, that he might be turned back. Our fields have been divided; because of this you will have no one casting the cord in the inheritance. What we set at the end of the section according to the Hebrew, in the assembly of the Lord, for which the Seventy translated in the Church of the Lord, is, according to the common edition, the beginning of the following section. And therefore we shall discuss it there, if the Lord commands. Woe, therefore, to you, peoples of the Jews, who both devise evil and complete it in deed. And the beds given you for rest you pollute with debaucheries, and whatever iniquity you plot at night, as if it were not permitted to put it off, you hasten to fulfill as soon as the day has dawned, not considering that your hand is strong against God. And in order that Scripture might teach what it was that they devised at night and did by day, it sets it out part by part. They coveted, he says, fields and took them by violence, and houses, it is understood, they coveted, and those which they had coveted they plundered; and not only did they wrong men and their houses, but they also laid waste with rabid mouth their descendants, who deserved mercy because of their tender age.

But this same thing can also be taken of the last captivity, that all things befell them because they crucified the Lord, yet in such a way that it is the edition of the Seventy translators that is expounded. For the glory of the daughter of Israel has been made bald and shorn over her once most delicate sons, and if any hair grew back afterwards, it was cut off in turn by another shaving and shearing. Then all their counsels were turned into toil, and what they devised, with mind and spirit asleep, brought them toils; and what they had done was thrown into confusion as soon as the light of Christ and vengeance appeared. For though they had read that Israel conquered when Moses lifted up his hands to the Lord, and was overcome by Amalek when Moses let his weary arms sink, they did not lift up their hands to the Lord, but, perpetrating every crime against the poor and the people of the Lord, they desired fields, and plundered the houses of orphans, and laid waste alike a man and his wife and his children and his substance.

But if we wish to follow the third exposition, of which I spoke above, that the whole discourse is directed to the human soul, which, falling from paradise, has come into the captivity of this world, we shall see that all our thinking is toil and pain, and our beds are full of evils, and the very light that is seen is mixed with darkness, and what we plot at night we accomplish in gloom. For who of us lifts holy hands to God without anger and scheming? Who does not desire the estates of this world, forgetful of the possessions of paradise? You may see some joining field to field and boundary to boundary, and the lands of cities not sufficing for the small little body of a man.

I have expounded, as far as the narrow limits of my slender wit allowed, both the first captivity, by the Assyrians and Babylonians, and the second, by the Romans, because they crucified the Lord, and the third, the spiritual one, by which each one of us fell with Adam from paradise and lives in the captivity of this world; from which, when the Lord comes, he will raise up those who are crushed, and loose those in fetters, and lead back into his own possession those who were once the devil's captives, and the speech of the Psalmist will be fulfilled, who says: Ascending on high, he led captivity captive. According to this exposition, a fourth captivity can also be understood with regard to the Church, from which each one goes out through sin, and afterwards is led back into Jerusalem by Ezra, which means helper, that is, by the word of God. But if anyone, meditating on the law of the Lord day and night, has had greater zeal, greater talent, leisure and grace, and can say something more probable about the present section, I do not envy him, I do not scorn him; rather, I desire to learn from him what I do not know, and I will gladly profess myself his pupil, provided he teaches and does not disparage. For nothing is so easy as for a man at leisure and asleep to dispute about the labors and vigils of others.

Since, therefore, you have done these things and devised what is useless, I too, the Lord, will devise evil against this family; not that what I devise is evil, but that what I inflict seems evil to those who suffer it; and it will so press upon you that you cannot lift your necks, nor walk proudly, you, namely, whom the time of captivity had oppressed.

Therefore the Lord devised evils against that tribe, by no means against the twelve tribes, but against the tribe of malice, befouled in crime, from which they could not lift their neck, nor walk upright. In short, to the present day they are subject to the Roman Empire, and are pressed down by the yoke of captivity, and do not lift their necks. As for what follows, ἐξαίφνης, that is, suddenly, it is not found in the Hebrew scrolls, and yet it can fit the present passage, so that we say: Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I devise evils against this tribe suddenly, from which they cannot lift their necks, and for this reason they will not be able to lift them, because the time is evil. For just as they worked evils against the Lord Jesus, so they will endure the evils of perpetual captivity, and will come into such great distress that all their songs and psalms will be turned into mourning.

Therefore the Lord devises evils against us, from which we cannot lift our necks, nor walk upright, for it is a most evil time, according to the words of John, who says: The world is set in wickedness. The same thing is signified also by that daughter of Abraham in the Gospel, a noble soul, whom Satan had bound and bent over, and who could not be raised up on high before the coming of the Lord, nor look up at her Creator. Hence the Savior says: This woman, he says, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound, ought she not to have been loosed from this bond on the sabbath day?

Then a parable will be spoken over you, and your miseries will be turned into a song: We have been laid waste with devastation, the portion of my people. My temple, he says, which alone I had more than the other nations, will be changed into a ruin. How will the Assyrian depart from me, when he returns to distribute my fields to himself by lot? Therefore, O family of Israel, against which I devise evil, you will have no part in the inheritance of the just.

And the people will know how to say nothing else but this: In misery we have been made miserable. For the land of promise, which had earlier been divided by lot to two and a half tribes beyond the Jordan, with Moses casting the cord, and afterwards apportioned by Joshua son of Nun to the remaining tribes, has been divided among the nations by a Roman surveyor, and there was no one to forbid; rather, though it holds all the nations, there is no one of the Jews who possesses the ancient soil in its former freedom.

Since, therefore, all our glory has been shorn, and we have enlarged our shaving, or our widowhood — for so it is found in some codices —, men have been sent to mourn us with Jeremiah, and to take up a parable over us, and to say with the Apostle: I shall mourn many who have sinned and have not repented. For who would not mourn, seeing human souls possessed like assorted household goods by demons and various vices? One demon, that of fornication, casts the cord; another, that of avarice; that one, of murder; this one, of perjury, stretches out the lines. The portion of the people of God has been divided by the cord, and the fields once of holiness and of paradise, with whose fragrance Isaac was delighted in his son Jacob, have been handed over to the Assyrians and to the Babylonian king. And while the foxes have holes and the birds of the air nests, The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

The Church, then, is commanded not to have sadness and anxiety over the affairs of the world and the losses that are wont to happen in this world, and it is said to her inhabitants: O you who are in the Church of the Lord, rejoice always, and whatever befalls you from the judgments of God, give thanks for it. Nor do I say this because you ought not to weep — for Blessed indeed are those who weep, for they shall laugh —, but I warn you of this, that you do not lament over the things that are of the world. If one of your kin has died, if the treasury has seized your property, if gout or any other disease whatever has oppressed your body, do not weep, do not shed tears, and do not consider the present but the future, and be weighed down rather because you dwell longer in this tabernacle of death. Rather beware of this, that you do not insult those who fall, and think another's ruin your own edification; let each one measure himself by his own strength, not by the weakness of another. Otherwise what justice is this, for the branches of the wild olive to insult the branches of the olive, which were broken off because of their unbelief, and to say: The house of Jacob provoked the Spirit of the Lord to anger, killing the prophets, worshipping idols, crucifying the Son of God? He who does this will not be free from reproach, and with the measure with which he judged he will himself be judged, and just as he speaks of the sins of the one who falls, so another will insult his ruin.

So much according to the Hebrew understanding; but the Seventy translators in this place do not cohere with themselves at all. For to what was set first, In the Church of the Lord do not weep, what consequence is there, that there should be added, for he will not cast off the reproaches which he speaks: The house of Jacob has provoked the Spirit of the Lord? And also what follows: If these are his devices, are not his words good with him, and have they walked upright? What bearing on the later part have the words that are said: And formerly my people stood out as an adversary against its own peace; they flayed off its skin, to take away the crushing of war? It seems to me, however, that in a place so very difficult the sense can be rendered or expressed thus, if only the prudent reader will acquiesce in our reasoning.

Do not speak, speaking; it will not drip upon these, confusion will not overtake them, says the house of Jacob. Is the Spirit of the Lord cut short, or are such his thoughts? Are not my words good with him who walks uprightly? And on the contrary my people has risen up as an adversary; you have taken away the cloak from over the tunic, and those who were passing by in simplicity you have turned into war. LXX: In the Church of the Lord do not weep with tears, nor let them lament over these things? For he will not cast off the reproaches, which he speaks: The house of Jacob has provoked the Spirit of the Lord, if these are his devices; are not his words good with him, and have they walked upright? And formerly my people stood out with enmities against its own peace; they flayed off its skin, to take away hope, the crushing of war. Do not speak, he says, speaking, for which Aquila translated: Do not drip, dripping; at times by a Hebrew idiom calling eloquence a dripping, from the fact that it flows and reaches the ears of those who hear, in the likeness of descending rain. Do not deceive yourselves, O house of Jacob, and say to one another for mutual consolation: God is good, the captivity which we fear will not come.

But some one will say to me, You adduce a thing strange to me, when you call the Son the Word. For John indeed speaks of the Word, but it is by a figure of speech. Nay, it is by no figure of speech. For while thus presenting this Word that was from the beginning, and has now been sent forth, he said below in the Apocalypse, "And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and He that sat upon him (was) Faithful and True; and in righteousness He doth judge and make war. And His eyes (were) as flame of fire, and on His head were many crowns; and He had a name written that no man knew but He Himself. And He (was) clothed in a vesture dipped in blood: and His name is called the Word of God." See then, brethren, how the vesture sprinkled with blood denoted in symbol the flesh, through which the impassible Word of God came under suffering, as also the prophets testify to me. For thus speaks the blessed Micah: "The house of Jacob provoked the Spirit of the Lord to anger. These are their pursuits. Are not His words good with them, and do they walk rightly? And they have risen up in enmity against His countenance of peace, and they have stripped off His glory." That means His suffering in the flesh. And in like manner also the blessed Paul says, "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak, God, sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteousness of the law might be shown in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit." What Son of His own, then, did God send through the flesh but the Word, whom He addressed as Son because He was to become such (or be begotten) in the future? And He takes the common name for tender affection among men in being called the Son. For neither was the Word, prior to incarnation and when by Himself, yet perfect Son, although He was perfect Word, only-begotten. Nor could the flesh subsist by itself apart from the Word, because it has its subsistence in the Word. Thus, then, one perfect Son of God was manifested.

Will his generous mercy and his most clement Spirit, which has risen widely and abundantly upon all, be cut short and be severe in us alone? Or are his thoughts of such a kind as we see in men, so that he holds on to an old anger and is roused to vengeance by sudden fury? To this the Lord answered: I am indeed good, and my words sound clemency, but to those who walk on the right road.

There follows: If these are his devices: are not his words good with him, and have they walked upright? That the Jewish people stumbled, he says, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might come in, belongs to the dispensation of God, so that afterwards, when Israel believes, all might be saved, and all might stand in need of the mercy of God. Hence the Apostle too, coming to the question of this place, proclaims that the depth of the wisdom and knowledge and of the judgments of God is an unsearchable abyss. If, then, it is God's devices and thoughts that the former branches of the olive should be broken off and others from the wild olive grafted in, you ought not to insult but to fear lest you fall, nor should you suppose that you please God in this, if you read his words, that is, his scriptures. The scriptures profit the reader only if what is read is fulfilled in deed. If, speaking of the scriptures, you can say: Or do you seek a proof of him who speaks in me, Christ? The Lord indeed will give the word to those who preach the gospel with great power, and upon a high mountain has he gone up who preaches the gospel to Zion, and he lifts up his voice in strength who preaches the gospel to Jerusalem. And in this way the words of God are good, if they are with him, that is, if God does not desert the preacher whose heart and lips agree. But he who confesses with his lips while his heart is far from God, and recounts his justices and takes up his covenant in his mouth, and is defiled with the filth of sins, with him the words of God are not good. This is to be said not only of the sinner, but also of him who does not have spiritual grace, that is, the grace of prophecy and of teaching and of interpretation, and of the greater charisms. This must be said, that if a man of this kind wishes to give the causes of the elements and the reason for his faith, and to explain why God, who is good and the Creator of all, came to the Jews alone and called the nations only in the last age, he does not have the good words of God with him, but out of his own unskillfulness defiles even those words of God which are good, words which walk upright and require upright ears. And these things indeed the Lord commands the people that succeeded, and the Church gathered from the Gentiles: not to insult the former generation, and so by insulting not be free from reproaches.

But he who, I do not say long ago, but yesterday, worshipped idols in insult to me, and, as far as lay in him, seized tyrannical arms against me; who stripped the unhappy people of God's help, and took away the cloak as if from over the tunic; who turned against me in war all the simple among the believers and those who rest in the authority of their elders, will not the Lord drip upon him, and will not confusion seize him? But as for what we have translated, And on the contrary my people has risen up as an adversary, since the word mul signifies both the contrary and yesterday, Symmachus rendered it more plainly, so as to say: One day before, my people stood out as an enemy, in order to resolve the question, namely that God was imputing to the people not past vices but recent ones, and such as seemed to have been committed as if yesterday.

And he himself, who is the true judge and speaks without perturbation, relates how in his passion Israel was contrary to him, and did this not because it could harm its Creator, but because it perpetrated everything against its own peace. Hence too the word to Jerusalem: If you knew the things that are for your peace. And with their peace lost, they flayed off their own skin, that is, they took away from themselves the help of God by which they were protected, and left their flesh as it were bare, without skin and covering, so that whatever seemed beautiful while the mercy of God covered it from above, this, when that mercy withdrew, displayed ugliness to those who saw it. And when peace and the help of God withdrew, because they had resisted the Lord, of whom it is said, The Lord who crushes wars, the Lord is his name, they could not resist their adversaries, but were defeated in every contest, nor was there anyone to crush the wars springing up against them, in respect of both persons of the enemies, either the men who led them captive, or the strength of the adversaries who daily slaughtered their souls by blasphemy.

Let him who cannot fly like an eagle fly like a sparrow. Let him who cannot fly to heaven fly to the mountains. Let him flee before the valleys that are quickly destroyed by water. Let him pass over the mountains. Abraham's nephew passed over the mountain of Segor and was saved. But Lot's wife could not climb it, for she looked back in womanly fashion and lost her salvation. "Draw near the everlasting mountains," the Lord says through the prophet Micah, "arise from here, for this is not a rest for you by reason of uncleanness. You have been corrupted with corruption, you have suffered pursuit."And the Lord says, "Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains." Mount Zion is there, and so is the city of peace, Jerusalem, built not of earthly stones but of living stones, with ten thousand angels and the church of the firstborn and the spirits of those made perfect and the God of the just, who spoke better with his blood than Abel. For the one cried out for vengeance but the other for pardon. The one was a reproach to his brother's sin; the other forgave the world's sin. The one was the revelation of a crime; the other covered a crime according to what is written, "Blessed are they whose sins are covered."

You have cast out the women of my people from the house of their delights; from their little ones you have taken away my praise forever. Arise and go, for you have no rest here; because of its uncleanness it will be corrupted with a most grievous rotting. The translation of the Seventy — if indeed it is the Seventy's; for Josephus writes, and the Hebrews hand down, that only the five books of the law of Moses were translated by them and handed over to King Ptolemy —, differs so much in the present place from the Hebrew truth that we can neither set out the heads side by side nor explain their meanings together. Therefore let our translation be discussed first, and afterwards we shall come to them. The word is still against the people of God, to whom he had already said above: On the contrary my people has risen up as an adversary: from over the tunic you have taken away the cloak; namely that they had not only done this, but had also made the women, that is, the matrons once delicate, go into captivity, or, under a metaphor, the cities of Judea, which in Isaiah too he calls the daughters of Zion, because Zion was their metropolis. From their little ones too, he says, you have taken away my praise forever: no one remained among the people, all being either killed or captured, who sang my psalms; and even the few who survived in Babylon testify that they cannot sing. How, they say, shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?

LXX: The leaders of my people will be cast out of the houses of their delights; because of their evil devices they have been cast out. This can be taken both generally of the princes of the Jewish people, the priests and Pharisees, who after the passion of the Lord were cast out of the city of their delights, in which they had formerly wantoned because of their evil devices; and specially of the stock of David, because as soon as the Lord was born, the prince failed from Judah, and the leader from his thighs, when he came for whom it was reserved, and the expectation of the nations appeared. But the prophetic word also describes the princes of the Church who abound in delights and believe that they keep their chastity amid feasts and wantonness: that they are to be cast out of their spacious houses and sumptuous banquets, and dishes sought out with great labor, and cast out because of their evil thoughts and works. And if you wish to know whither they are to be cast out, read the Gospel: Into the darkness namely without, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Is it not a confusion and a disgrace to preach Jesus crucified, the poor and hungry master, with stuffed bodies, and to set forth the doctrine of fasting with red cheeks and swollen faces? If we are in the place of the apostles, let us not only imitate their speech, but also embrace their way of life and their abstinence. Holy, certainly, is the ministry of the apostles also, to minister to widows and the poor. It is not right, they say, that we should leave the word of God and serve tables. But now the priest of Christ invites to dinner, I do not say the poor, I do not say the brethren and those who cannot invite in return, from whom, apart from the grace, episcopal hands could hope for nothing else, but soldiers and men girt with the sword, and judges, with centurions and squadrons of soldiers keeping watch before their doors. The clergy run about the whole city, seeking to provide for the judges what they either cannot find in their own praetoria or at least do not buy up once found. Nor indeed is it to be thought that this invective is directed generally at everyone, but rather that the prophetic word strikes those who are such, and threatens them with punishments and everlasting darkness, so that those who are not restrained by shame and modesty may repent at least at the threat of penalties.

LXX: Draw near to the eternal mountains. By the eternal mountains we can understand either angels or prophets, of whom it is also written in the psalm: Its foundations are on the holy mountains, and in another place: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help will come to me. And he draws near to the eternal mountains who is not separated by his sins from the fellowship of the blessed, just as Moses too drew near to God, not in place but in merit. And to those who drew near to the eternal mountains the Lord himself spoke: I am a God who draws near, and not a God from afar. The mountains are called eternal to distinguish them from those which are not eternal, namely the princes of this world, the dark mountains; and when these have been lifted up like the cedar of Lebanon, they pass away with the world, and their place cannot be found.

Arise, therefore, and go into captivity, for you have no rest in this land, which has been polluted because of your crimes and cannot be cleansed unless it first keeps a long sabbath. And the reason I say to you, you have no rest here, is that your land is polluted and will be corrupted with a most grievous rotting, namely by captivity, either the Babylonian or the Roman, because it drank the blood of the Lord; for it can be understood according to either truth of the history.

LXX: Arise and walk, for there is no rest for you here.
