For just as sometimes it is the bishop's fault, sometimes the people's, and often the teacher is answerable for the sin, often the pupil, and now it is the father's failing, now the son's, according as they are taught well or badly, so in the judgment of God the charge will be referred either to the angels, if they have not done all that belonged to their office, or to the people, if, while the angels did everything, they themselves scorned to hear. There are some who interpret the mountains and hills and strong foundations of the earth as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the rest of the patriarchs, before whom, as hearers called together to the judgment, the case of the people of Israel is to be argued. Others think the mountains, hills and valleys are angels, as we said above, who either serve God in the heavenly places, or preside over men upon this earth, or, being set in the underworld, are called the foundations of those who through their own fault became earthly; of these foundations of the earth we find it written elsewhere too: A fire is kindled from my fury, it will burn down to the underworld below; it will devour the earth and its foundations. The strong and ancient foundations of the earth — on account of which the earth has not passed away until now, and, hanging over the void, stands balanced — are the merits of the just, of whom the Apostle speaks: Built upon the foundations of the apostles and prophets. Just as, then, the apostles and the prophets and the whole choir of martyrs are the strong foundations of the earth, so, according to the LXX, the valleys and precipices, which in Greek are more expressively called φάραγγες, are the foundations of those who have received the image of the χοϊκοῦ (of the earthy one). The judgment of the Lord, therefore, will be decided with his people, and with Israel. He who, as God, could inflict punishments for the crimes of a sinful people does not wish to appear powerful, but just, and he summons the sinners to judgment, according to that prophetic word: Come, and let us judge, says the Lord; even now he presses the people of Israel, in the presence of the angels and of all creation, to answer if it has anything to answer, so that God may be justified in his words and may prevail when he is judged.

Would you like me to utter to you the words of God to Israel, stiff-necked and hardened? "O my people, what have I done to you, or in what way have I injured you, or wherein have I wearied you?" This language indeed is more fit from me to you who insult me. It is a sad thing that we watch for opportunities against each other and having destroyed our fellowship of spirit by diversities of opinion have become almost more inhuman and savage to one another than even the barbarians who are now engaged in war against us, banded together against us by the Trinity whom we have separated. We are not foreigners making forays and raids upon foreigners or nations of a different language, which is some little consolation in the calamity. But we are making war upon one another, and almost upon those of the same household. Or if you will, we the members of the same body are consuming and being consumed by one another. Nor is this, bad as it is, the extent of our calamity, for we even regard our diminution as a gain. But since we are in such a condition and regulate our faith by the times, let us compare the times with one another; you your emperor, and I my sovereigns; you Ahab and I Josiah.
AGAINST THE ARIANS AND ON HIMSELF, ORATION 33:2

The third interruption of the Prophet is that, as he is stationed among people who exercise wickedness, he desires to be separated from their contamination. Many think that this refers to the Lord Jesus, because it is His alone not to fear judgment, since He conquers when He is judged. For He has a judgment from an unjust man, into which Christ willingly enters, as you have written: My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I saddened you? Moreover, when the father gives all judgment to him, not as if to an infirm person, but as if to a son, because he himself can undergo judgment? If they think that the judgment of the Father must be undergone by the Son, then the Father surely does not judge anyone, but he has given all judgment to the son; so that everyone may honor the son just as they honor the father. The father honors the son, and do you judge? We have said this so that no one would consider us as placing the person of the Prophet in the place of the Lord due to fear of questioning, when the holy David, foreseeing by the spirit that the Jews would rise up against the passion of the Lord, does not fear the judgment of his faith: he even demands that his cause be distinguished from the nation of persecutors; so that he would not be entangled with the descendants of his wicked generation and the heirs of his posterity, the lineage of the whole Jewish race.

God, therefore, speaks to the people of Israel, and summons them to judgment, and grants them leave to dispute against him. My people, what have I done to you that I ought not to have done? Or how have I grieved you? although this is not found in the Hebrew. But a father grieves the son he has scourged, and the shepherd visits the iniquities of the sheep with the rod. In what have I been troublesome to you? Or, as is written more expressively in the Hebrew, with what toil have I oppressed you? Or will you interpret my benefits as an insult, and, longing for the melons and the meats of Egypt, will you grieve that you were brought out of the land of Egypt and freed from the house of bondage by my help, because I gave you as leaders Moses my friend, and Aaron my priest, and Miriam my prophetess?

But we who long to contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, and truly have Abraham as our father, let us hear God, when we have sinned, disputing against us and reproving us by the greatness of his benefits. For we once served Pharaoh, and made mud and bricks for the Egyptian people, and he redeemed us who gave himself as a redemption for all, so that we who had been redeemed by the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemies and whom he gathered from the regions, might say: For his mercy is forever. He also sent before our face Moses, the spiritual law, and Aaron, the great priest, not bearing the typical ephod and the truth, but having on his forehead the seal of holiness which God the Father sealed. And he sent Miriam, the prophecy of the prophets; and not only did he grant us this, but he also freed us from the hands of the enemies.

"For the Lord will judge his people, and he will [give] comfort among his servants." The reason for the previous praise is stated: "For the Lord will judge his people," that is, the Jewish people, to whom he revealed great miracles and assigned his prophets so that the people would not sin. He also sent to them his own Son, so that their accursed hardness could finally be melted. But because they persisted with accursed obstinacy, he will certainly judge them, because they were unwilling to be his, though he had chosen them from all nations as his possession. To them he says, "Hear, O people, and I will speak," and elsewhere, "My people, what have I done to you?" So he will judge them. But hear what follows as it concerns the faithful: "He will again have compassion upon us." He means when he will render their promised rewards to those on earth afflicted with harsh contempt on account of his name. Scripture says of them, "Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted," and in another place are the words "He that believes in me is not judged but will pass from death to life. But he that does not believe is already judged."

You see the Lord is teaching you a lesson, challenging you to goodness by his own example, teaching you even when he reproves. When accusing the Jews, for instance, he says, "O my people, what have I done to you? Or wherein have I grieved you? Or wherein have I offended you? Answer me. Is it because I brought you out of the land of Egypt, and delivered you out of the house of bondage?" adding, "And I sent before your face Moses, Aaron and Miriam. O my people, remember what Balak king of Moab devised." You were indeed oppressed, an exile in foreign lands, laden with heavy burdens.

For the torrent of cords, or of thorns, Symmachus rendered the valley of thorns. Now there is a place near Livias, beyond the Dead Sea, six miles distant from Livias, where Israel once committed fornication with the Midianites. This place the prophet Micah mentions in the person of God, saying: My people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam son of Beor answered, from Settim to Gilgal. For which there too the Seventy translated ἀπὸ τῶν σχοίνων, that is, from the cords to Gilgal.

My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I been troublesome to you, answer me, for I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and from the house of servants I freed you, and I sent before your face Moses, and Aaron and Miriam. My people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab devised against you, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Shittim to Gilgal, that you might know the justices of the Lord. LXX: My people, what have I done to you, or how have I grieved you, or in what have I been troublesome to you? Answer me: for I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and from the house of bondage I redeemed you, and I sent before your face Moses, and Aaron and Miriam. My people, remember what Balak king of Moab devised against you, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Schoenis to Gilgal, that the justice of the Lord might be known. For justices or justice Symmachus rendered mercies, and where the LXX has Schoenis, all rendered the Hebrew itself, Settim. Now it is a place in which Balak king of the Moabites gathered an army against Israel, ὁμώνυμος (of the same name) with the trees which even today grow throughout the desert of Mount Sinai. For where in the LXX the ark of the covenant, or the altar and the tabernacle, and the other things which are reported to have been made of incorruptible wood are mentioned, in the Hebrew Settim wood is set down, which has the likeness of the tree that we commonly call the white thorn. Hence I think that the LXX too rendered σχῖνον, that is, the mastic tree, but that gradually, through the error of copyists, it came about that σχοῖνοι, that is, ropes, was read instead of σχίνοις, that is, mastic trees.

But if this seems little to you, remember that time when Balak king of Moab hired Balaam the diviner for a fee against you, and see how, against his own will, the soothsayer, wishing to curse you, blessed you; from Shittim to Gilgal, surveying with his eyes the whole army of Israel and changing places, as if I could not go with him as he went and pass over with him as he passed over; and this I did so that my mercies and justices might be known to you, for I love you so much that, while I am cursed daily by the mouth of blasphemers, I did not allow you to be cursed by the enemy. The Hebrews expound this passage, in which it is said: From Shittim to Gilgal, that you might know the justices of the Lord, thus: From the time when you committed fornication in Midian until the time when Saul was anointed king at Gilgal, recall to memory what evils you have done, and how great the good things I have done for you, and you will know my mercy toward you. Let this be what God spoke to carnal Israel according to the history.

For let us remember what he devised against us who wished to devour us and lick up our congregation: the true Balak, the devil. For Balak is interpreted ἐκλείχων, that is, licking up, king of the paternal water; since Moab, according to another etymology, is called paternal water. When, therefore, Balak was lying in wait for us, and lying in wait through his vain people, which is what Balaam is interpreted, God did not allow us to lie under his curses, but on the contrary there blessed us, compelled by the truth of the thing itself, the vain people of the nations, born of him who is in the skin — for Beor is interpreted in the skin — ever given over to the flesh and to the works of death; and the vain people, sprung from him who is wholly in the skin, answered on our behalf, always changing places, or standing upon thorns, or upon cords, so that we may follow the error of the common edition too. Now thorns, according to the Savior's words, are the cares of this world, and riches, and pleasures, in which the vain people is. And that it stands in ropes, namely in the bonds of sins — for with the ropes of his own sins each one is bound — Isaiah also is witness, saying: Woe to those who drag out their sins like a long rope, and iniquities like the strap of a heifer's yoke. If, then, it stands, it stands only on thorns and on ropes; but if it wishes to go around, it has no steady step, but, always wavering and tottering, it comes as far as Gilgal, which is interpreted κυλισμὸς, that is, rolling, or a wallowing-place. Whenever we see some rising up against us, and thirsting for our blood with greedy jaws, and, by an unforeseen dispensation of God, those who had come against us coming over to our side, let us say: Balaam came from the cords as far as Gilgal, that the justice of God may be known.

Is everyone who is turning from sin to faith, turning from sinful practices (as if they were his mother) to life? I shall call in evidence one of the twelve prophets, who says, "Am I to make an offering of my firstborn son for my impiety? Should I offer the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul?" Can the mother buy her way to God by giving up her firstborn? This must not be taken as an attack on the words "increase in numbers." Micah is naming, by using the word impiety, the first impulses after birth, which do not help us to knowledge of God. If anyone misuses this as a basis for saying that that birth is evil, he should also use it as a basis for saying that it is good, in that in it we come to know the truth. "Come back to a sober and upright life and stop sinning." But the sinner knows nothing of God. "We are not wrestling against flesh and blood but against spiritual beings, potent in temptation, the rulers of this dark world," so there is forbearance. This is why Paul says, "I bruise my own body and treat it as a slave, because every athlete goes into total training." By "total training" we understand not that he abstains from absolutely everything but that he shows self-control in those things he has taken a deliberate decision to use. "They do it to win a crown which dies, we for one which never dies," if we win the contest. No effort, no crown!

Then the word of the prophet, a little further on, suggests again the curtailing and abolition of the ancient ritual of the Law, speaking in the person of the people:

"6. Wherewithal shall I reach the Lord, and lay hold of my God most high?. Shall I reach him by whole burnt-offerings, by calves a year old? 7. Should I give my firstborn for my ungodliness, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?"

And he makes this answer to them in the person of God:

"8. Has it not been told thee, O man, what is good? And what does the Lord require of thee, but to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to be ready to walk after thy God? "

You have then in this prophecy of the Descent of the Lord among men from heaven, many other things foretold at the same time, the rejection of the Jews, the judgment on their impiety, the destruction of their royal city, the abolition of the worship practised by them of old according to the Law of Moses; and on the other hand, promises of good for the nations, the knowledge of God, a new ideal of holiness, a new law and teaching coming forth from the land of the Jews. I leave you to see, how wonderful a fulfilment, how wonderful a completion, the prophecy has reached after the Coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ.
The Proof of the Gospel, Book 6, Chapter 13

For what is asked of you, O man? Only that you fear God: seek for him, walk after him, follow in his ways. "With what shall I win over the Lord? Shall I win him over with burnt offerings?" The Lord is not reconciled, nor are sins redeemed, with tens of thousands of young goats or thousands of rams or with the fruits of unholiness, but the grace of the Lord is won with a good life.

What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord? Shall I bend the knee to God most high? Shall I offer him burnt offerings, and yearling calves? Can the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams, or with many thousands of fat he-goats? Shall I give my firstborn for my crime, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul? LXX: With what shall I lay hold of the Lord? Shall I receive my God most high? Shall I lay hold of him with burnt offerings, with yearling calves? Will the Lord accept, with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of fat he-goats? If I give my firstborn for impiety: the fruits of my womb for the sin of my soul. God had summoned the people to judgment; the people, knowing its sin, does not wish to contend, but to entreat, and yet even in its very prayers it has no confidence. For there is nothing worthy that can be offered to God for sin, and no humility can wash out the stains of offenses, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and of calves, and burnt offerings full of marrow, and the gore of rams and of fat he-goats, to wash away the filth of the soul. Shall I, he says, give my firstborn for my crime, as the king of Moab is described as having done? Or the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul, as Jephthah did, offering his daughter for the rashness of a vow? We, therefore, who are of the people of God, knowing that there shall not be justified in the sight of him anyone living, and saying: I have become a beast before you, repenting for our sins, hesitate and say: With what shall I lay hold of the Lord? Shall I receive my Lord most high? How shall I be able to hold him as he flees? With how great purity shall I be able to prepare a lodging for the Trinity? Or shall I lay hold of him with burnt offerings, so as to offer my whole self to him as a burnt offering, or with yearling calves, so that, leaving milk and coming to solid food, I may be made worthy of the acceptable year of the Lord? If I offer a thousand rams, if ten thousand he-goats, and, understanding them spiritually, display in myself all the victims of Leviticus, and a thousand fall at my side, and ten thousand at my left, yet I shall be able to give nothing worthy with which to lay hold of God or receive him. If I give my firstborn for impiety, and the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul, I shall indeed give whatever is first in me, but for my sin and impiety I shall offer nothing worthy to God. Hence David also prays and says: Wash me more and more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I know my iniquities, and my offense is ever against me. For the sin of the soul blood alone is worthily offered, and the blood that is worthily offered is not that of calves, not of rams, not of he-goats, but one's own, as the prophet says and asks: What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? And afterwards answers: I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord. Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints. Yet even this very blood we do not give, but give back. And what is there alike? When the Just One has died for sinners, the Son of God for men, shall we, sinners and men, die for the confession of his name?

"But God,"[adulterers and fornicators say,] "is good and most kind." He is "merciful, compassionate and rich in mercy," which "he prefers to every sacrifice." "He desires not so much the death as the repentance of the sinner." He is "the Savior of all people, and especially of the faithful." Therefore the children of God must also be "merciful" and "peacemakers," "forgiving each other as Christ also forgave us," "not judging, lest we be judged." For to "his master a man stands or falls; who are you to judge the servant of another?" "Forgive, and you will be forgiven." Yet many such things as these are only said, not done, merely bandied about, unmanning rather than strengthening discipline, flattering God and pandering to themselves.

"You have been told, O man, what is good. And what does the Lord require of you, but to do justice, to love mercy and to be prepared to walk with your Lord?" Accordingly, the gospel says to you, "Arise, let us go from here," while the law says to you, "You shall walk after the Lord your God." You have learned the method of your flight from here—why do you delay?

I will show you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you: surely to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk carefully with your God. LXX: It has been declared to you, man, what is good, or what the Lord requires of you, except that you do judgment, and love mercy, and be ready to walk with your God. Since you are in doubt, O people of Israel — or rather the whole human race, for I am by no means speaking to the people of the Jews, but my speech will run out generally to every man — how you can appease God for your sins, if you do not even have victims by which your impiety may be compensated, I will answer you what God requires; indeed, I have already shown it before in the law. For it is written in Deuteronomy: And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, and walk in all his ways, and love him; and serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord your God and his justifications, whatever I shall command you today, that it may be well with you? The Lord requires of us, and, counting our salvation necessary, asks to receive what profits the giver: that we do judgment, that is, that we do nothing without reason and counsel, so that the mind first judges what it is going to do and afterwards completes it in deed; that we love mercy, and are merciful not as if compelled or out of necessity, since God loves a cheerful giver. Nor let us say: Go today, and come back tomorrow, and I will give to you. And when we have done judgment and loved mercy, what reward shall we receive? We shall walk with the Lord God, as Enoch, according to the faith of the Hebrew scrolls, walked with God, and pleased him, and he was not found, because God translated him. For you said: With what shall I attain to the Lord, or with what shall I lay hold of him? I promise you more: do judgment, and love mercy, and you will walk with your God. Or certainly, to walk with God is not a reward but a precept. For just as we are commanded to do judgment and to love mercy, so it is enjoined that we be prepared to walk with the Lord our God; we ought to sleep at no hour, to be secure at no time, but always to expect the householder's coming and to dread the day of judgment, and in the night of this world to say: I sleep, and my heart keeps watch. The word esne, which the LXX translated 'to be ready', and we 'to walk carefully', Theodotion expressed more significantly: καὶ ἀσφαλίζου τοῦ πορεύεσθαι μετὰ Ἐλωαὶχ, that is: And take careful heed that you walk with your God, or, as the Fifth Edition translated: καὶ φροντίζειν, namely to act carefully, and to have this care, that you walk with your God. For he who says that he believes in Christ ought so to walk as he also walked. And the apostle Paul: Be imitators of me, he says, as I am of Christ.

Forget about burnt offerings, countless sacrifices and oblations of firstborn, he is saying. If you are concerned to appease the divinity, practice what God ordered you in the beginning through Moses. What in fact is that? To deliver fair judgment and decision in all cases where you have to choose better from worse, to continue giving evidence of all possible love and fellow-feeling to your neighbor, and be ready to put into practice what is pleasing to God in every way. He means, in short, "You will love God with all your heart, all your mind and all your soul, and you will love your neighbor as yourself," as was said of old through Moses. Do this, he is saying, as something preferable to sacrifices in God's eyes.

You ask what you should offer: offer yourself. For what else does the Lord seek of you but you? Because of all earthly creatures he has made nothing better than you, he seeks yourself from yourself, because you have lost yourself.

A brother asked a hermit, 'Tell me something good that I may do it and live by it.' The hermit said, 'God alone knows what is good. But I have heard that one of the hermits asked the great Nesteros, who was a friend of Antony, 'What good work shall I do?' and he replied, 'Surely all works please God equally? Scripture says, Abraham was hospitable and God was with him; Elijah loved quiet and God was with him; David was humble and God was with him.' So whatever you find you are drawn to in following God's will, do it and let your heart be at peace.'
The Desert Fathers, Sayings of the Early Christian Monks

A hermit was asked by a brother, 'How do I find God? With fasts, or labour, or vigils, or works of mercy?' He replied, 'You will find Him in all those, and also in discretion. I tell you many have been very stern with their bodies, but have gained nothing by it because they did it without discretion. Even if our mouths stink from fasting, and we have learnt all the Scriptures, and memorized the whole Psalter, we may still lack what God wants, humility and love.'
The Desert Fathers, Sayings of the Early Christian Monks

Here is a priest who serves at every hour with great fear while walking humbly with the Lord his God in accordance with the word of the prophet. Meanwhile another priest is hardly capable of having that much fear even when he is about to die and enter into the last judgment before his Lord. But the full expression of the priesthood is comprised of the combination of the teaching of truth with good works. This is in accord with blessed Luke's comment that in writing his Gospel he had composed a treatise concerning all the things that Jesus began both to do and to teach.

Let us therefore return to the beginning of the section. And, discussing it first according to the letter, let us, with the help of your prayers, strive to attain the spiritual sense. Hear, ten tribes of Samaria, what the Lord solemnly declares to you: Still there is fire, that is, iniquity, in the house of the ungodly Omri, and the treasures of ungodliness persist in the royal house. Do you wish to hear, one by one, the evils of which your city is full? Learn: a scant measure that provokes the wrath of God, a deceitful balance and differing weights, and men who sell their wares by one weight and buy by another. And if indeed the poor were doing this, their want could have defended the crime by necessity. But as it is, her rich men are full not so much of riches as of iniquity, because all riches, while they despoil others, are begotten by iniquity. Lying follows the amassing of riches, and the hand accustomed to storing up treasures possesses a deceitful tongue. Truth begets poverty, lying begets riches.

Thus far we have set out what seemed right to us according to the Hebrew; now, returning to the translation of the LXX translators, let us discuss each point as best we can. The Samaritan tribe, which cut itself off from the people of God, is called to hear. And it is told: In vain you fashion idols, you put together golden calves with a craftsman's hand, and in imitation of Jerusalem you wish to build another metropolis; for who will be able to adorn the city? Can fire, which is kindled by the flaming darts of the devil, and the house of the wicked man, which according to its hardness and impenitent heart treasures up for itself wrath on the day of wrath, and of the revelation of the just judgment of God? And injury increases iniquity, so that it not only plunders from the house of God, which is the Church, but also lays waste what belongs to others with pride and haughtiness. Can he be justified who, without balance and weight, fraudulently gathers his riches from the testimonies of the Scriptures, riches which are treasures of iniquity? For although the Lord commands: There shall not be in your bag a great weight and a lesser, these men, for the sake of shameful gain, always respect persons in judgment, and in the same case judge rich and poor now one way, now another, not according to the matter but according to the difference of their means; and the inhabitants of their city, which they think they are adorning with depraved doctrines and perverse teaching, speak lies, and set their mouth on high, and despise the simplicity of the people of the Church.

The voice of the Lord cries to the city, and there will be salvation for those who fear your name. LXX: The voice of the Lord will cry to the city, and he will save those who fear his name. In the Hebrew this is the beginning of the next section, but with the Seventy translators it is the end of the preceding one; and it has this sense: Your God asks nothing else of you, O man, except that you do judgment, and love mercy, and be ready to walk with your God. For the voice of the Lord is heard in his city, the Church, and resounds daily in the holy Scriptures, so that not only those who love mercy, but also those who are lower and still fear the name of the Lord, may be saved by his teaching and clemency. But if it is the beginning of the following section, let us refer it, according to the history, as said to Samaria, the metropolis of the ten tribes, which was captured while Micah was prophesying, and let us say: The Lord rebukes Samaria and threatens her with the blows that are to come, so that the people of Judah, or those who fear the name of the Lord, hearing that others suffer punishments, may themselves be seized with fear and obtain salvation. For when the pestilent man is scourged, not only the wise man but even the fool will become more prudent. And you will refer this very thing to sinners in general and to the just, so that the torment of some may become an example to the rest. This indeed the Lord also explains in the Gospel concerning those on whom the tower in Siloam had fallen: that they were not the only sinners in the whole people, but that their punishment was meant to provoke the rest to repentance.

When your princes were doing this, I did not wish to overthrow you at once, but little by little I began to strike you and to warn you with various blows. I sent famine upon you, I sent thirst, I sent diseases, and devastation by the enemy round about; the crop did not bring forth grain, the pressed olive did not yield oil, barren vintages denied the wine. Against the iniquities, and the deceitful measures, and the fraudulent weights, I brought these punishments.

Hence the most merciful God does not strike them all at once, but strives little by little to admonish them through blows, saying: And I will begin to strike you with ruin on account of your sins; and the sense is: O city which the heretics wish to build, I will strike you so that you perish, not unto abolition, but in so far as you are a sinner.

There follows: You shall eat, and not be satisfied. For they read and do not understand; and feeding on the words of the Scriptures, they suffer a want of truth. And I will cast out, he says, you; and you shall lay hold, and shall not save; and whoever shall be saved shall be handed over to the sword. I will abandon you, he says, to your own judgment; and after you have sought many things and found nothing, understanding your error, you will see that you cannot be saved by all your doctrines. But whoever think themselves satisfied, and have not been cast out from themselves, nor have grasped the truth, will be handed over to the sword, and will be instructed by punishments.

You shall sow, therefore, O tribe, and O most wicked city, which the heretics build with fire, and iniquity, and insults, and a deceitful balance, and a fraudulent bag; you shall sow, and not reap; you shall press the olive, and not be anointed with oil; and the grapes, and not drink wine. Indeed it profits you, once your error is recognized, that you may not have disciples, that you may not anoint your head with the oil of sinners, that you may not make drunk with the wine of Sodom those who drink it.

Hear, O tribes, and who will approve it?

Still there is fire in the house of the ungodly, treasures of ungodliness, and a scant measure full of wrath. Shall I justify an ungodly balance and the deceitful weights of the bag? By which her rich men were filled with iniquity, and those who dwell in her spoke lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth. And I therefore have begun to strike you with ruin for your sins. You shall eat and not be satisfied, and your humiliation is in the midst of you; and you shall lay hold and shall not save; and those whom you save I will give to the sword. You shall sow and not reap, you shall tread the olive and not be anointed with oil, and the must, and not drink wine. And you have kept the precepts of Omri and every work of the house of Ahab; and you have walked in their wills, that I might give you up to ruin, and those who dwell in her to hissing, and you shall bear the reproach of my people. LXX: Hear, O tribe, and who will adorn the city? Is it fire, and the house of the wicked man treasuring up wicked treasures, and iniquities with injury? Shall the wicked man be justified in the balance, and deceitful weights in the bag, from which they have filled up the riches of their ungodliness, and those who dwell in her have spoken wicked things, and their tongue is exalted in their mouth. And I have tormented you with ruin on account of your sins; you shall eat, and not be satisfied; and I will cast you out into yourself, and you shall lay hold, and shall not save; and whoever shall be saved shall be handed over to the sword; you shall sow and not reap; you shall press the olive and not be anointed with oil; and the grape, and not drink wine; and the statutes of my people shall be scattered, and all the works of the house of Ahab; and you have walked in their counsels, that I might hand you over to ruin, and its inhabitants to hissing, and you shall receive the reproaches of the peoples. In this section the LXX disagree greatly with the Hebrew truth, and most of all at the beginning: Hear, O tribe, and who will adorn the city? And the statutes of my people shall be scattered. In place of which we have put, for the sake of the coherence of the discourse: And you have kept the precepts of Omri, although in the Hebrew too it is written: And the precepts of Omri have been kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab. For if Ammi had been written in the Hebrew, the LXX would rightly have translated it 'of my people'; but as it is, since Amri is written, with the letter res added, it denotes not the name of the people but the father of Ahab, of whom the history of Kings relates, and no one is in doubt that it is an error. In short, after the father's name the son is placed, and it is said: And all the works of the house of Ahab.

But because you kept all the ceremonies of idolatry which Omri, the ungodly king, had established, and observed every work of the house of Ahab and Jezebel in place of my law, I was driven by your crime to give you and your inhabitants up to hissing, and that you should bear the reproach of my people, while, taken captive by the Assyrians, you are conquered as if you were the people of God, and on your account my name is blasphemed among the nations. It should be noted in the present passage that where we read: And you shall bear the reproach of my people, or, as the LXX translated: You shall receive the reproaches of the peoples, Ammi is written in the Hebrew for 'of my people'. If, then, Ammi means 'of my people', no one doubts that above, for Amri, 'my people' was wrongly translated.

And the statutes of my people, or of Omri, shall be destroyed, and all the works of the house of Ahab, of those who stood forth as patriarchs and princes in the heresies. These we can refer either to the contrary powers or to the heresiarchs, such as were Marcion and Basilides, and recently Arius and Eunomius. And you walked in their wills, namely those of Omri and Ahab. And he says well, in their wills. For the teaching of wicked masters is not the teaching of God, but the inventions of their heart. And I will hand you over to ruin, so that you perish in so far as you are heretical. And your inhabitants to hissing, either so that you may follow the hissing of the good shepherd, according to Zechariah, who says: I will hiss for them and gather them, because I have redeemed them. Or surely to the hissing of the dragon, that is, to the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved, and that, being corrected, they may learn not to blaspheme. And they will suffer all this so that they may understand their error, that they have borne the reproaches and sins of all nations and of many peoples. I know that some have referred to the Church what we have interpreted of the heresies. But how the name of Omri and Ahab, princes of Samaria, can be referred to Jerusalem and Judah, under whose names the Church is interpreted, I do not well understand.
7: Who is speaking when the prophet says, "Woe is me, soul, for I have become one as gathering straw in harvest?" For did the prophet literally "gather" or even want to "gather"? Does the prophet have a farm? Anyway, the only one who rightly gathers from what has been planted for harvest is not the prophet but the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Since there are many faults among the pagan nations but also among those who are supposed to be from the church, the prophet laments and mourns for our sins when he says, "Woe is me, for I have become as one who gathers straw." Let each of us scrutinize himself. Is he an ear of corn? Will the Son of God discover something in him to pick or harvest? Do we find that some of us are those swept by the wind? Even as we have still a little in ourselves, two or three kernels, our sins are many against us. Seeing that the churches, or those so-called, are filled with sinners, he says, "Woe is me, for I have come as one who gathers straw in the harvest and as one gathering grape gleanings in the vintage." [The Lord] comes seeking fruit on the vine, for each of us is planted also as a vine "in a fertile place" or as a vine "transplanted out of Egypt," yet planted to bear fruit. He comes, he seeks in what way to pick, he discovers some "grape gleanings" and a few "clusters," neither flourishing nor plentiful. Who among us has "clusters" of virtue?

The unjust are scattered like chaff, while the just are like wheat. Finally, listen to the words of the Lord to Peter: Behold, Satan has desired to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. Those who are scattered like chaff will fail; but not the one who is like that grain which fell and rose again, enriched by the abundant yield of many fruits. Therefore the Prophet says: Woe is me, for I have become like one gathering straw in the harvest! Therefore, straw that is quickly burned is compared to impiety and to dust. Therefore, after he said: They will be like chaff carried away by the wind, he added the verse immediately saying: Or like the dust that the wind snatches away. Finally, so that you may know that the wicked person quickly grows weak and vanishes like dust, you have the following statement in the first Psalm: Not so the wicked, not so, that is, not like the righteous: but like the dust that the wind scatters away from the face of the earth.

Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers the clusters of the vintage in autumn. There is no cluster to eat; my soul desired the first-ripe figs. The holy man has perished from the land, and there is no upright one among men. All lie in wait for blood, a man hunts his brother to death. The evil of their hands they call good; the prince demands, and the judge is for requiting, and the great man has spoken the desire of his soul, and they have troubled it. He who is best among them is like a brier, and he who is upright like a thorn from the hedge. LXX: Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble in the harvest, and like clusters in the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat the first-ripe; which my soul has suffered. Woe is me, O soul, for the reverent man has perished from the land, and there is none among men to correct; all are judged in blood, each one afflicts his neighbor with affliction, they prepare their hands for evil; the prince demands, and the judge has spoken peaceful words, it is the desire of his soul. And I will take away their goods like a devouring moth, and walking upon a rule in the day of your watching. Having foretold the captivity both of the ten tribes and of the two — for the word of the Lord came to Micah of Moresheth concerning Samaria and Jerusalem — the prophet laments that no just man from the people is found in the land who could withstand the wrath of God and set himself in the midst like a wall. In vain, he says, have I spoken; in vain have I wished to seek, as it were, the last clusters of the city already stripped of its vintage and ruined, and, since there is no cluster to eat, at least to take as food the unripe figs, which the Hebrews call bechchora, that is, the green fruit of the fig; as if he were saying: Finding no bread, because of the greatness of the famine I sought out refuse and bran.

Moreover, according to the Seventy, who disagree in certain points and at the end of the section translated altogether differently, the sense seems to me to be of this kind. The prophetic word, or the apostolic, laments over the human race in general, that the word has cast the seed of doctrines in vain, and that, instead of crops and grain, the late reaper has found scarcely empty stubble and hollow stalks, and has not been able to find even small clusters in the vineyard, and the rest up to the end of the section. For if he is blessed who speaks into the ears of one who listens, and the ear of the hearer is the desire of the wise man, and an understanding hearer is the joy of the speaker, on the contrary a bad pupil is the teacher's grief; and the words of Jeremiah also agree with this complaint: I have not profited, nor has anyone profited me. There are some who think this is said in the person of the Savior, complaining that in so great a multitude of believers, and in the whole world of the human race, he scarcely finds works worthy of his blood, he who also says in Psalm 29 (30): What profit is there in my blood, while I go down into corruption? Others, however, assert that it by no means befits his person to say: Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble in the harvest, he who said in the Gospel: Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for reaping. And elsewhere: The harvest indeed is great, but the laborers are few. Those, then, who wish it to be understood in the person of the Savior say that it is no wonder if he says: Woe is me, he who both wept over Jerusalem and shed tears at the death of Lazarus. But that too, I have become like one who gathers stubble in the harvest, they refer to the consummation of the age, which they also meaningfully interpret as the harvest; and they say that this prophecy can be fulfilled at that time when, iniquity having multiplied, the love of many will have grown cold, and the Son of Man, when he comes, will find faith rare upon the earth; for then, like stubble after the harvest and like clusters after the vintage, scarcely will any be found among them who have kept the faith amid the devastation of all; and they think that this utterance, spoken in the person of the man who was assumed, is confirmed by what follows: Woe is me, O soul, the soul of which he was speaking: My soul is sorrowful, even unto death.

Cain and Abel followed in the generation of humankind, and Cain was the first murderer. Afterwards a deluge engulfed the earth because of exceeding wickedness of humanity. Fire came down from heaven upon the people of Sodom because of their corruption. Subsequently God chose out Israel, but even Israel became perverse and the chosen race was wounded. For, while Moses stood on the mountain before God, the people worshiped a calf in place of God. In the days of their lawgiver Moses, who said, "You shall not commit adultery," a man dared to enter a brothel and be wanton. After Moses, prophets were sent to heal Israel, but in their exercise of healing they deplored the fact that they could not overcome evil, so that one of them [Micah] says, "The faithful are gone from the earth, among men the upright are no more!" The psalmist says, "All alike have gone astray; they have become perverse; there is not one who does good, not even one." And again, "Cursing, and theft, and adultery, and killing have overflowed" upon the land. "They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons." They engaged themselves in auguries and enchantments and divinations; and again, "They fastened their garments with cords and hung veils next to the altar."

The holy man has perished from the land, and there is no upright one among men; everywhere ambushes, everywhere fraud, innocent blood is shed, for avarice and lust brotherhood is disregarded; and they not only do evil things but also defend them, and, exchanging the names, they say that what is evil is good. The princes themselves do not receive gifts from those who offer them, but compel their subjects to give, and demand them. And the judge is for requiting, judging another in the same way as he himself is judged by another, so that they may grant one another's crimes mutual favor and defend themselves in another's crime. Whoever is great and, as it were, most learned in the law speaks not God's will but his own. And they have troubled it, either the city or the truth, or the land, of which it is said above: The holy man has perished from the land.

The one returning has perished from the land, either because the Antichrist kills the saints, or because all fall away at the greatness of the stumbling-blocks. And there is none among men to correct; all are judged in blood, not in light and small sins, but in the greatest and in those that concern blood. Not neighborliness, not friendship, not kinship will hold back the crime; all will raise their hands to evil, so that even he who has not been able to do evil nevertheless sins by his will while he prepares his hands. The prince himself asks, and the judge speaks peaceful words; for he receives gifts, the desire of his soul. Since this is plain, and I am wary of the ill will of princes and judges, I leave it to the reader's understanding and will add only this: Gifts blind the eyes even of the wise; they also give life to a soul to which they ought not to have given life, and kill the soul that lives by its own merit and virtues, and they do this for the sake of gifts which they shamelessly demand and more shamefully receive.

Now we must discuss it according to the earlier interpretation, in which we spoke of the heretics: Hear, O tribe, and who has adorned the city? Is it fire and the house of the wicked? And again, of the Church: Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble in the harvest. And once more: Woe is me, O soul, the reverent man has perished from the earth, and there is none among men to correct. And thereafter: The prince asks, and the judge has spoken peaceful words, by the desire of his soul. Hence a double curse follows: Woe, woe, your vengeances have come; now shall be their lamentation, and let us say that it is written of the heretics: Do not believe in friends, O simple peoples, and in depraved leaders who promise that they are friends and princes of the heresies; for they seek not your salvation but their own gains, and they trample the deceived flock under their feet; and in her who sleeps with you beware of believing anything; I can understand her to be nothing other than the flesh, so that we may not readily believe the blandishments of the flesh, lest the hardness of the mind and its manly constancy, subdued, should grow soft by her allurements.

For he who is best among them is like a brier, pricking and holding fast, wounding whoever comes near it and seizing him with a hooked tooth; and he who has been found upright is like a thorn from the hedge, so that pain is found where help was thought to be. This according to the Hebrew.

These the Lord threatens, saying: And I will take away their goods, which they think goods, which seem goods to them. But in the truth of the matter those things will never be called goods which both despoil the giver and kill the receiver; although it is not so much a threat as a blessing to take away evils from them, and for the Lord himself and the divine word to enter into their consciences and, like a moth, to devour whatever is perverse, and to lay waste their plunder and their evil thoughts, and to walk upon the norm and rule of truth, drawing back to what is right those very men who were led by depraved opinions; and to do this in the light of truth, and on that day when those who are holy and chosen from the Church will go up to the watchtower and, in the loftiness of their doctrines and works, will discourse on heavenly things.

The day of your watching, your visitation, comes; now shall be their devastation.

Do not believe a friend, and do not trust in a leader. From her who sleeps in your bosom guard the bars of your mouth, for the son does insult to the father, and the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man's enemies are his own household. But I will look to the Lord, I will wait for God my Savior; my God will hear me. LXX: Woe, woe, your vengeances have come, now shall be their weeping; do not believe in friends, nor hope in leaders. From her who lies with you, beware lest you believe her, for the son does insult to the father, and the daughter rises against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man's enemies are the men of his own household. But I will gaze upon the Lord, I will wait for God my Savior? My God will hearken to me. Except for the beginning of the section, in the remaining parts both editions agree; and for the present, according to the history, he signifies the day of the watching of Samaria, or of Jerusalem, which she had often expected and feared would come, and her visitation, the captivity, saying: Your laying waste comes; now shall be their devastation, that is, of the inhabitants, or their siege: for mabucha in the Hebrew means rather πολιορκίαν and φρούρησιν, that is, siege and guard, than devastation.

There follows the exposition of the Seventy, who said: Woe, woe, your vengeances have come, that is, the punishments that are to be inflicted for crimes. To me, he says, belongs vengeance, and I will repay, says the Lord. And in another place: The days of your retribution have come. For the Lord executes vengeance for those who cry out to him day and night and say: How long, O Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth? Therefore the vengeances have come, and now shall be their weeping, that is, the weeping of the vengeances, so that those who laughed before may lament, and, as soon as they go out of the world, may endure torments, such as that rich man, once clad in purple and abounding in delights, endures in hell, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. But as for what follows: Now shall be, understand it either of the end of each one's life, or of the consummation of all things and the day of judgment, when general vengeances will come upon all.

Thus far it is commanded that we should not readily believe friends, leaders, wives. And a reason is given that does not quite answer to the proposition; for he says: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises against the mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies are his own household. For what has it to do with a friend, a leader, a wife, if son and daughter and daughter-in-law rise up against father and mother and mother-in-law? It seems to me, therefore, that it can be joined with what precedes in this way. Do not believe friends, and leaders, and wives, who can change and are only for a time, since even son and daughter, forgetting their upbringing and their infancy, rise up against the authors of their life and of their bodies, and do insult to those whom it is a crime to hurt even by a look. But this exposition by no means fits the daughter-in-law rising up against her mother-in-law, and the man whose enemies are his own household. Terence in the Hecyra: What is this? All mothers-in-law hate their daughters-in-law; and although this is ambiguous, yet it is almost natural that the daughter-in-law should hate the mother-in-law, and the mother-in-law the daughter-in-law. So much for what the prophetic word may have described concerning the consummation and end of the world: what kind of generation is to precede the coming of the Antichrist.

Therefore believe none of the voices of the prophets, and do not lend your ear to the deceiving flattery of the diviners, for if among dear names and the affection of kinship faith is rare, how much more so among those who, flattering you, lie for their own booty, and, as for sick men, prescribe not what is useful, but what is delightful and pleasing. Do not believe a friend; for indeed Ahithophel rose up against David, and the true Ahithophel, Judas, against Christ. And do not trust in a leader, as the men of Shechem trusted in Abimelech. For they themselves made him king, and were oppressed by him. From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the bars of your mouth, lest you suffer what Samson suffered from Delilah.

Therefore do not believe friends, for every friend supplants with supplanting, and he who is a friend for the sake of something is not so much the friend of him whom he pretends to love, for a friend takes his name from love, as of the thing that he loves. A certain man, asked what a friend was, replied: Another self. But if the example of the Pythagoreans is set against us, who gave themselves to the tyrant as sureties for one another, we say that the sentence was pronounced by God not generally against all friends and the affections of love, nor against every time, but concerning that time of which the Apostle says: In the last days perilous times will come: for men will be lovers of themselves, covetous, disdainful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, not keeping covenant, informers, incontinent, harsh, without kindness, traitors, wanton, puffed up, lovers of pleasures rather than of God, and so on. For then brother will hand over brother, and father son, and mother daughter, and a man's enemies will be his own household. But even now faith is rare, when one thing is on the lips and another turns in the heart, and the honey of the tongue covers the poison of the mind. The rich have many friends, but from the poor even those who seem to be friends depart. Hence it is said: If you have a friend, possess him in temptation. I have read in someone's declamation: "A friend is long sought, scarcely found, hard to keep". Theophrastus wrote three volumes on friendship, preferring it to every other love, and yet he testified that it is rare in human affairs. There is also Cicero's book on friendship, which he entitled Laelius, in which that precept of our own writers, That a friend should be to us like old wine, and that we should drink it in sweetness, is set down in almost the same words. Friendship either finds equals or makes them; where there is inequality, the eminence of one and the subjection of the other, there is not so much friendship as flattery. Hence we also read elsewhere: "Let a friend be the same soul". And the Lyric poet, praying for a friend: Preserve, he says, the half of my soul. Do not, therefore, believe friends, that is, those men who seek gain from friendships. If you wish to delight in true friendship, be a friend of God, like Moses, who spoke to God as a friend to a friend. Be a friend, like the apostles, to whom the Savior says: No longer will I call you servants, because the servant does not know what his master does, but I will call you friends, because you have persevered with me in all my temptations. Dainty is the friendship that follows the good fortune and the riches of friends. Men of this kind seem to me to love not their friends but themselves. Let us consider more attentively the words of the Lord: But I will call you, he says, friends. And he gives the reasons why he calls them friends: Because you have persevered with me in temptation, and he did not stop there, but in all, he says, my temptations. For it sometimes happens that one who persevered with us in one temptation is overcome by others and withdraws. Secondly it is commanded: Nor hope in leaders: Cursed indeed is the man who puts his hope in man. Hope in man is vain, and true hope is in God. Hence Paul also says: And from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things. And the Lord himself through the prophet: The leaders of my people have not known me; they are foolish sons, and without understanding; they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have not known. They were indeed called my leaders, he says, and leaders of my people, but because they did not know me, and destroyed the name by their deeds, therefore they are foolish sons and without understanding; they have prudence only to this end, that they may subject the simple flock to themselves and trample it under their feet; but to do good and to rule the people they have not known. Do not believe in leaders: not in a bishop, not in a presbyter, not in a deacon, not in any dignity of men. Nor do I say this meaning that you ought not to be subject to ranks of this kind in the Church: Whoever indeed curses father or mother shall die the death; and the Apostle teaches that those set over us in the Church are to be obeyed; but I say it because it is one thing to honor leaders, another to have hope in leaders. Let us honor the bishop, defer to the presbyter, rise for the deacon, and yet let us not hope in them, for hope in man is vain, and sure hope is in the Lord. The third command: From her who lies with you, guard yourself, lest you believe her. Hence the apostle also calls women the weaker vessel, and commands that honor be shown them by their husbands. For man was not created for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man, and: The wife, he says, is to fear her husband. It belongs to the wife to fear, and to love her husband with fear. To husbands it belongs only to love, because love is of the perfect: Husbands, he says, love your wives and do not be bitter towards them, even though they provoke you to anger and do such things as to deserve to endure bitterness. For this is what παραπικραίνεσθαι means; yet do not repay them in kind with bitterness. And Solomon too, in Ecclesiastes: And one man, he says, out of a thousand I found, and a woman among all these I did not find; taught perhaps by his own example that women, through whom he had offended God, are not to be believed. And the sublime poet too — not another Homer, as Lucilius supposes of Ennius, but the first Homer among the Latins —: A varied and changeable thing ever is Woman.

The Greek and Latin histories are full of how many men were deceived by their wives and had their lives betrayed. From the Scriptures, moreover, the examples both of Delilah, whom we mentioned above, and of another woman before Delilah bear witness, who wrung from Samson his secret of seven days by her tears, and by feigned love discovered what lay hidden. Hence Samson afterwards says: If you had not tamed my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle.

Before all things however we ought most carefully to observe the Evangelic precept, which tells us to enter into our chamber and shut the door and pray to our Father, which may be fulfilled by us as follows: We pray within our chamber, when removing our hearts inwardly from the din of all thoughts and anxieties, we disclose our prayers in secret and in closest intercourse to the Lord. We pray with closed doors when with closed lips and complete silence we pray to the searcher not of words but of hearts. We pray in secret when from the heart and fervent mind we disclose our petitions to God alone, so that no hostile powers are even able to discover the character of our petition. Wherefore we should pray in complete silence, not only to avoid distracting the brethren standing near by our whispers or louder utterances, and disturbing the thoughts of those who are praying, but also that the purport of our petition may be concealed from our enemies who are especially on the watch against us while we are praying. For so we shall fulfil this injunction. "Keep the doors of thy mouth from her who sleepeth in thy bosom."
The First Conference of Abbot Isaac, Chapter 35

A threefold war is threatening us: domestic, civil, and military. The first is with the flesh, which has many troops. This servant-maid is ever-willing to give access, as did Eve. Hence, Against her who lies in your bosom guard the portals of your mouth.

Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword.  For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter in law against her mother in law.  And a man's foes shall be they of his own household. [Micah 7:6] He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me: and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.  And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me.  He that findeth his life shall lose it: and he that loseth his life for my sake shall find it.

Just what is the work of the axe? The excision of the soul that is incurably fruitless, like the tree even after the dung has been applied. And what does the sword do? The sword of the Word cuts through defenses. It does the work of separating the worse from the better. It actually creates a division between the faithful and the unbeliever. It may even stir up the son and the daughter and the bride against the father and the mother and the mother-in-law, the young and fresh against the old and shadowy. Accordingly, what is the latchet of the shoe, which you, John, who baptized Jesus, may not let loose? You who are of the desert, without food, you, the new Elijah, you who are more than a prophet, inasmuch as you saw him of whom you did prophesy, you the mediator of the Old and New Testaments. What is this latchet? It is precisely the message of the advent, the incarnation. No one can make it happen—neither those yet carnal and babes in Christ nor those who are akin to John in spirit.

A man, then, who remains the same and yet prattles to himself about the change for the better that he has undergone in baptism should attend to what Paul says: "If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself." For you are not what you have not yet become. The Gospel says of the regenerate, however, that "he gave all those who received him the power to become God's children." Now the child born of someone certainly shares his parent's nature. If then you have received God and have become his child, let your way of life testify to the God within you. Make it clear who your father is! The marks by which we recognize God are the very ones by which a son must show his relation to him. "He opens his hand and fills everything living with joy." "He overlooks iniquity." "He relents of his evil purpose." "The Lord is kind to all and is not angry with us every day." "God is straightforward, and there is no unrighteousness in him." This is what fathers do for children. Similar sayings are scattered through Scripture for our instruction. If you are like this, you have genuinely become a child of God. But if you persist in displaying the marks of evil, it is useless to babble to yourself about the birth from above.

For I have come to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man's enemies are those of his household. This passage is written in nearly the same words in the prophet Micah. And note, wherever a testimony is set down from the Old Testament, whether the sense alone agrees or the wording as well.

For the son does insult to the father; Absalom, namely, to David: he defiled not only the kingdom but also the concubines of his father by incestuous intercourse. The daughter rises up against her mother: although for the present we find no testimony of this in the holy Scriptures, there are so many examples of it in daily life that we ought rather to mourn that they are so many than to search for them. The daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, as the wife of Esau rose up against Rebekah. A man's enemies are the men of his own household. Here I do not seek examples, since there are too many of them for us to need testimonies.

For the son who was born of God, neglecting his Creator, blasphemes him by whom he was made, as Scripture says: Has not one God created you? Is not one the father of all of you? And the soul despises the heavenly Jerusalem, and scorns her mother the Church, and whoever despises her shall die the death. And the daughter-in-law rises up against her mother-in-law: this seems difficult to understand according to tropology; but whoever has read the Song of Songs, and has understood the bridegroom of the soul to be the word of God, and has believed the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which was published and which we lately translated, in which it is said in the person of the Savior: Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me by one of my hairs, will not hesitate to say that the word of God arose from the Spirit, and that the soul, which is the bride of the word, has as her mother-in-law the Holy Spirit, who among the Hebrews is called by a word of feminine gender, rua. Heretics, therefore, although they formerly believed in the Scriptures, which were written and published by the Holy Spirit, transfer themselves to new doctrines, and to the leaven of the Pharisees, and to the commandments of men, and while they despise the word of God, they do injury to their mother-in-law. And lest perhaps you doubt that the Word and Son of God is born of the Holy Spirit, consider the words of Gabriel to Mary: The Holy Spirit, he says, will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy thing that will be born of you will be called the Son of God. After this there follows: A man's enemies are the men of his own household. This it seems to us should be expounded thus according to tropology: The head of every man is Christ; and Christ is the head of the Church; his enemies are often those who are thought to be in his house, that is, in the Church, and they do not indeed withdraw from the head, but they think against their own head: those who, without a teacher and the grace of the Lord, promising knowledge of the Scriptures by their own judgment, are puffed up and know nothing; and they languish over questions and contentions and battles of words: those who, though they truly stand within the house, are enemies of the truth. We ought to know, moreover, that in the Gospel there are nearly the same words that we now read in the prophet, and that according to the context of that place they have another sense; whether they were taken from the prophet or commanded on his own authority, it belongs to the Lord to know, who spoke both in the prophets and in the Gospels. Now there the Lord says: I came to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies are his own household.

Since, then, these things are so, do not believe, Samaria and Jerusalem, the false prophets. But I, says the prophet, will look to the Lord; I will exult in God my Savior, or my Jesus, and my God will hear me.

These things having thus been set forth, if indeed we have been able to reach the sense of the Scriptures, the holy man, understanding that love has grown cold, and that at the consummation of the world men are not lovers of God but lovers of themselves, while others believe in friends and leaders and wives, and son and daughter and daughter-in-law rise up against father and mother and mother-in-law, and a man's enemies are his own household, himself believes in the Lord, and all his contemplation is in his God; and although he is pressed by the tribulations and pressures of the world, yet, having confidence in no one except him who says: Do not fear, I have overcome the world, he waits for God his Savior, and believing in him, and ever directing his eyes towards him, he hopes that he will be heard as often as he calls upon him.

Do not rejoice over me, my enemy; for though I have fallen, I will rise again. The ruin of weakness is not severe, if there is also not a desire to not rise from it. Have the will to rise, there is someone present who will make you rise.
Commentaries on the Twelve Davidic Psalms

Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise; when I sit in darkness: the Lord is my light. I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he judges my cause and executes judgment for me; he will bring me out into the light, and I shall see his justice, and my enemy will look on, and she will be covered with confusion, who says to me: Where is the Lord your God? My eyes will look upon her; now she shall be trodden down, like the mud of the streets, the day for your walls to be built. On that day the law shall be far off; on that day they will come even to you from Asshur, and as far as the fortified cities, and from the fortified cities as far as the river, and to sea from sea, and to mountain from mountain. And the land shall become a desolation because of its inhabitants, and because of the fruit of their thoughts. LXX: Do not insult me, my enemy, because I have fallen, and I shall rise again; for if I walk in darkness, the Lord will enlighten me. I will endure the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, and executes judgment for me, and brings me out into the light, and I shall see his justice, and my enemy will see me and confusion will cover her, who says to me: Where is the Lord your God? My eyes will see her, now she shall be for trampling, like mud in the ways, the day of the daubing of brick, your blotting out, and that day will thrust back your ordinances, and your cities will come into enclosure and into the division of the Assyrians, and your fortified cities into division from Tyre as far as the river, and from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain; and the land shall become a ruin with its inhabitants because of the fruits of their devisings. It seems to me that according to the letter Jerusalem is speaking against Babylon and the other nations which had insulted her: Do not rejoice at my ruin, for, the Lord having mercy, I shall rise; after I have sat in captivity he will bring me out of the darkness, and he will be my light. I will endure the wrath of the Lord, because I know that I deserved what I have suffered, until I am avenged on the nations, and judgment is executed for me. For I know that he will bring me out into the light and I shall see his justice, and my enemy Babylon will look on, and the other nations round about, and she will be covered with confusion, who now says insultingly: Where is the Lord your God? My eyes will see her, and not after a long time, but now and at present, trodden down like the mud of the streets.

Now let us come to the spiritual understanding, and, with the Holy Spirit himself expounding in what sense these things were written, let us toil even in the most difficult places. It seems to me that every soul, a Jerusalem in which the temple of the Lord was built, and the vision of peace, and the knowledge of the Scriptures, and which was afterwards overcome by sins, led into captivity and handed over to torments, speaks against Babylon, that is, the confusion of this world, and against the opposing power that presides over this world: Do not insult me, my enemy, because I have fallen, and I shall rise again; The Lord indeed lifts up those who are dashed down, and he speaks through the prophet: Shall he who falls not rise again? And: I do not desire the death of the sinner, only that he turn back and live. But if you despise me for this reason, that I endure torments, learn through Ezekiel that punishments are inflicted first on the holier, and that the Lord says: Begin from my holy ones. For if I walk in darkness, the Lord is my light. For although the rulers of this darkness have deceived me, and I sit in darkness and the shadow of death, and my feet have stumbled on the dark mountains, yet to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death a light has risen, and the light shines in the darkness. The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear; and I will speak to him and say: Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths. For he himself commanded me, placed as I am in the darkness of this age: Let your loins be girded, and burning lamps in your hands.

A different thing is death of the soul and complete destruction and total abandonment. This is known thereby that, although one falls, he does not forget the love of his Father; and although he is loaded with trespasses of every kind, his zeal for the service of good is not held back, nor does he desist from his course, nor abhor to stand in struggle against these things anew and with the same chance of being vanquished, nor cease from demolishing every day his building and beginning a [new] foundation.

And the word of the prophet is in his mouth: Till the hour of my departure from this world, rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light unto me. And he will not cease to struggle till death. He will not allow himself to be vanquished, as long as there is breath in his nostrils. And though his ship is wrecked every day and the sweat of his commerce becomes a prey to the depths, he does not cease to borrow and fit out ships and navigate with good hope; till the Lord, seeing his zeal, has mercy for his shipwrecks and inclines unto him in compassion and gives him strong impulses towards patience and towards braving the burning arrows of the Evil one. ‘This is wisdom from God and whoever is sick in this way, Is wise.

But there is no small danger of the mind falling into the error of supposing that every illness needs the aid of medicine. For not all illnesses come naturally, or from errors of diet or any other bodily causes, for which we see that the medical art is sometimes useful. For often illnesses are scourges of sins, sent to convert us. “For whom the Lord loveth, he chasteneth.” And “For this cause many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep. For if we discerned ourselves, we should not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world.” In such cases then we ought to be quiet and forbear medical treatment, and endure what comes upon us, when we have recognised our sins, as (Micah) said: “I will bear the indignation of the Lord, for I have sinned against him”; and we ought to show amendment by doing works worthy of repentance and remembering the Lord’s words: “Behold, thou art made whole; sin no more, lest a worse thing befall thee.”

There follows: I will endure the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, and executes judgment for me, and brings me out into the light; and I shall see his justice. All correction for the present seems to be a matter not of joy but of sorrow, but afterwards it will yield the peaceful fruit of justice to those who have been trained by it. The soul, therefore, perceiving that it has sinned, and has the wounds of sins, and lives in dead flesh, and needs cautery, says steadfastly to the physician: Burn my flesh, cut away the wounds, bind up all the humors and the noxious ῥεῦμα (flux) with a harsh draught of hellebore. It was my fault that I was wounded; let it be my pain that I endure so many torments, and afterwards receive health. And the true physician shows the soul, now safe and secure, the reason for the remedy, and teaches that he rightly did what he did. In short, after tortures and punishments, the soul, brought out of the outer darkness, and having paid the last farthing, says: I shall see his justice, and I will say: Your judgments are justified, O God. But if Christ has been made for us by God wisdom, and justice, and sanctification, and redemption, he who says that he sees justice after the wrath of God promises himself the sight of Christ. And this holds only of penitents. But it is much better not to have wounds, and not to need a physician. Healing is not the blessedness of those who are healed, but a solace after pain. Therefore let him who has been healed beware lest he sin again, and something worse befall him once more. We read in Leviticus, if indeed we read with open eyes, and the veil that is placed upon the law does not shut out the gaze of the inner eye, that leprosy is wont to arise in the weal and scar of a burn, and to change the color of the hair, and that a new foulness is added to the former disfigurement of the scar. This is so for this reason: that no one, secure about repentance because after sin he can say: I will endure the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, should sin and need cautery, and, once healed, be wounded again.

But when the Lord has brought us out into the light, and we have seen his justice, then our enemy Babylon will see, and will be covered with confusion, she who formerly said to us: Where is your God, thinking that Jerusalem after her wounds could not be healed. And our eyes will look upon her, and she will be trodden down like the mud of the streets.

Thus far Jerusalem has spoken, or the prophet in the person of the people; now God is brought in answering Jerusalem: O Jerusalem, the days have come for your walls to be built, which had been destroyed by the Babylonian when he laid you waste.
