On that day the law shall be far off, or the precept and command, as Symmachus and Theodotion translated, saying ἐπιταγὴν καὶ πρόσταγμα; and the sense is: You will by no means lie subject to the rule of the Babylonians; on that day on which your walls will be built, they will come to you from Asshur, and from the fortified cities; from the fortified cities, I say, as far as the Jordan, across which the people also passed before, and from the Red Sea; and from all the nations as far as the Dead Sea, which is near your land, and to Mount Zion, from the mountains of the Persians and the Medes, into which they had earlier been carried away; and the land will be the remnant of the Chaldeans, and of those who had laid you waste, a desolation, because of its inhabitants, and because of their evil works. This the Jews promise themselves to this day; and in that place in which we have expounded: On that day the law shall be far off, as it seemed to us, and as the more prudent among them discuss it, some lie frivolously and say: On that day on which the walls of Jerusalem have been built by Christ, the holy Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets, which are now held by us, will be taken out of our hands and handed over to the people of the Jews.

And since every end of punishments is the beginning of good things, and pain advances toward health, bricks will be made from her mud, and her daubing will be the shaping of bricks. And on that day she will cast off her old errors, and her cities, which had been badly fortified, will come into enclosure, or into division, and will be divided by the Assyrians; from Tyre too, which is interpreted συνοχὴ, that is, distress, other powers will rise up, and there will be sedition even as far as those who delight in the flux of this age and beget lusts in men. And from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain, wars will rise up against one another, so that bitterness fights against bitterness, and a loftiness that exalts itself and is to be humbled contends against another height; and then truly it may be fulfilled: Come, let us go down and confound their languages, so that each may not hear the voice of his neighbor; for indeed it is profitable that the most wicked powers should have no concord among themselves. And when Satan has been divided against Satan, then at last his whole kingdom will be destroyed. And what frequently happens in great armies, that when the tyrant has been killed his attendants divide the kingdom among themselves and rise up against one another, and there is civil war among them, this will happen also at the consummation of the world, when the walls of Jerusalem have been built, and Babylon has fallen, and the Assyrians, and the Tyrians, from the river, and from the sea, and from the mountains, that is, all the nations of demons, will fight among themselves; and, their kingdom having been scattered, the kingdom will be the Lord Jesus', and every knee shall bow, of things in heaven, and on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. But that you may know that the end of this sedition is the advance of the virtues, the land of Babylon will then become a ruin with all its inhabitants, and will by no means bear Babylonian fruits.

For as to what is said according to the Seventy, The day of the daubing of brick, your blotting out, let us understand that it is said not to Jerusalem, as we expounded according to the Hebrew, but still to Babylon: that she too is to be blotted out, and trodden down like brick. And that day will thrust back the ordinances: not the ordinances of God, but those ordinances which, O Babylon, you had commanded to be observed against the law of God.

And your cities will come into enclosure, or into division, with the Assyrians attacking you — since indeed Babylon was a city of the Chaldeans, not of the Assyrians —. And your fortified cities will be for the division of a hostile army, from Tyre as far as the river Tigris, by which you are encircled, and from the Great Sea as far as the Red Sea, which, on the flank, for those traveling to India, touches your regions. And from mountain to mountain; namely, from the mountains of Judea as far as the mountains of Media and of the Persians, all Mesopotamia and the whole region which is now held by you in the middle will be subjugated to the rule of your adversaries. And the land shall become a desolation because of the most wicked fruits of your pursuits. Where the Seventy translated from Tyre, let us know that in the Hebrew there is written masor, a word which, if it is divided into the preposition Ma and the noun Sor, is understood as from Tyre; but if it is one word, it means a fortification. In short, all rendered περιοχὴν, καὶ περίφραγμα, καὶ πολιορκίαν, not from Tyre, as the LXX did, but a fortification and the circuit of a walled city. Let this, according to the Hebrew and the hopes of carnal Israel and of the people of the concision, be what our leisurely discourse has played through as a prelude, as it were from superfluity.

Shepherd your people with your rod, the flock of your inheritance, dwelling alone in the forest in the midst of Carmel; they shall feed on Bashan and Gilead according to the days of old, according to the days of your going out from the land of Egypt; I will show him wonders. The nations shall see, and shall be confounded at all their strength. They shall put their hands upon their mouth; their ears shall be deaf. They shall lick the dust like serpents, like the creeping things of the earth; they shall be troubled out of their dwellings. They shall dread the Lord our God, and they shall fear you. LXX: Shepherd your people with your rod, the sheep of your inheritance, dwelling alone in the forest; in the midst of Carmel they shall feed on Bashan and Gilead according to the former days, and according to the days of your going out from the land of Egypt; I will show them wonders. The nations shall see, and shall be confounded in all their strength; they shall put their hands upon their mouth; their ears shall be deaf. They shall lick the ground like serpents that drag the earth; they shall be troubled in their enclosures; at the Lord our God they shall dread, and they shall be in fear of you. As to what is said, Shepherd your people with your rod: God the Father is speaking to the Son, that is, to our Lord Jesus Christ, that, since he is the good shepherd and lays down his life for his sheep, he should shepherd his people with his rod, and the sheep of his inheritance. And lest we think that the peoples are the same as the sheep, we read in another place: But we are your people, and the sheep of your pasture. "People" refers to all who are rational, but "sheep" to those who, not yet using reason, are content with simplicity alone, and are called of the inheritance of God. But the people as much as the sheep need the shepherd's rod, of which the Apostle too speaks: What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity and the spirit of meekness? For this reason, I think, because the people of Israel was stiff-necked and was always sighing for the meats of Egypt, Moses used, not only against the Egyptians, whom he struck with ten plagues, but also against the people in the wilderness, the rod of the law, a rod that strikes and breaks all the earthen and fragile vessels; but from the apostles of the Lord the Savior, who spoke wisdom among the perfect, the rod was struck out of their hands, because perfect love casts out fear. But if anyone objects to us how it can now be said to Christ, that is, to the good shepherd, who is certainly greater and better than the apostles, that he should use a rod, when it is a mark of greater progress to have no rod than to correct peoples and sheep with a rod, we shall answer them according to what the Lord promises his apostles, that they would do greater signs among the peoples than he himself had done. And because the Lord was still speaking to carnal Israel, and not yet to the one who could perfectly know the mysteries, for that reason it was said of him that he should shepherd his people and his flock with the rod, but that the rod was struck out of the hands of the apostles, and the severity of the law tempered by the clemency of the Gospel. Moreover, these peoples and these sheep will be struck, and will be shepherded with the rod, for this reason, that they had dwelt alone in the forest. This we can indeed take also of those who, separating themselves from the Church, give themselves up to the banquets and friendships of the Gentiles, and also of those who out of hatred of the human race seek a solitary life, such as we read that Timon was at Athens; not that the solitary and prophetic life which Elijah and John had is to be condemned, but because, if someone, despising the rest, is himself proud and dwells in the forest of vices, he must be corrected with the rod. He who dwells alone and does not dwell in the forest is in the praise of virtues; but he who is alone and does not do the works of justice, and enjoys only the pleasure of quiet, and does not toil in the work and labor of Christ, nor seek his food with his own hands, as the Apostle commands, and is lifted up into pride, he dwells in the forest and moves among the fruitless trees. But yet, because he is the good shepherd, and his rod strikes for this purpose, to amend, the prophetic word promises better things, and says: In the midst of Carmel they shall feed on Bashan and Gilead, according to the days of eternity, and according to the days of your going out from Egypt. Carmel means knowledge of circumcision, Bashan confusion, and Gilead transmigration of testimony. Therefore the people of God, and the sheep of his pasture, which before were fed apart from the Lord's flock and outside his Church, and moved about in the forest of errors, will afterwards be transferred to the knowledge of the true circumcision, and will serve God in the spirit, and will glory in the Lord, and will not trust in the flesh, and will be the true circumcision, and not the concision. And when they have been fed with the spiritual circumcision, understanding their former sins, they will be confounded in their vices, and will blush, and will be in the confusion that leads to life; for there is also another confusion that leads to death, in which Og, king of Bashan, once dwelt, since Bashan means confusion; and from this worst confusion the Lord also promises that he will free his people: The Lord said: From Bashan I will turn back, I will turn back from the depths of the sea. And when we have known the true circumcision, and have been confounded over our sins, then we shall be in Gilead, which means transmigration of testimony, in the Church of Christ, into which the testimonies of the law and the utterances of the prophets have passed over; and this will be done for us according to the days of old, according to the days when we went out from the land of Egypt, of which Moses says: Remember the days of eternity, not the days of this age, which are called evil, but the everlasting days. And he remembers the days of eternity who does not look at present things, and has risen with Christ, and sits with him in the heavenly places, already anticipating in mind that he has been freed from the days of the present age.

The divine word also promises that he will show wonders to his people and to the sheep of his inheritance: Then, he says, the nations shall see, and shall be confounded in all their strength, because they had once laid waste and prevailed against the people of God; and their confusion will bring them progress, when they have understood their own evils. For they will put their hands upon their mouth, and their evil works will take from them all freedom of speaking. But just as the hands of the impious nations close their mouths, so the hands of the just will open their mouths, as they receive from good work the faculty of speaking with God. Their ears too will grow deaf, because malice has not only blinded the gaze of the eyes but has also made the ears grow deaf; for they would not hear the voice of the charmers, and of the sorcerer who charms wisely. And according to Isaiah: With their ears they heard heavily, although it is much less to hear heavily than not to hear at all, and to become deaf so as not to hear the word of truth.

Hear what is even more wonderful, that the hidden and veiled mysteries of the ancient books are in some degree revealed by the ancient books. For Micah the prophet speaketh thus. “According to the days of thy coming out of Egypt will I show unto him marvellous things, etc.…In this Psalm, therefore, although the wonderful spirit of prophecy doth look into the future, yet it seemeth, as it were, to be merely detailing to the past. “Judah,” he saith, “was His sanctuary: the sea saw that and fled:” “was,” “saw,” and “fled,” are words of the past tense; and “Jordan was driven back, and the mountains skipped, and the earth trembled,” in like manner have a past expression, without, however, any difficulty in understanding by them the future.…For though it was so long after the departure of that people from Egypt, and so long before these seasons of the Church, that he sang what I have quoted; nevertheless, he witnesseth that he is foretelling the future without any question. “According to the days,” he saith, “of thy coming out of the land of Egypt will I show unto him marvellous things.” “The nations shall see and be confounded.” This is what is here said, “The sea saw that, and fled:” for if in this passage, through words of the past tense the future is secretly revealed, as is the case; who would venture to explain the words, “shall see and be confounded,” of past events? And a little lower down he alludeth more clearly than light itself to those very enemies of ours, who followed us flying, that they might slay us, that is, our sins, which are overwhelmed and extinguished in Baptism, just as the Egyptians were drowned in the sea, saying, since “He retaineth not His anger for ever, because He is of good will and merciful, He will turn again, He will have compassion upon us, He will drown our iniquities: and Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.”

And these things will happen so that the nations may see, and be confounded in all their evil strength, and put their hands upon their mouth, and grow deaf in their ears, and lick the earth like serpents that drag the ground, so that first they may be shut in, and, once shut in, be troubled, then, terrified, be astonished before the Lord God of the saints, and at last they too may fear him. This is according to the LXX. Moreover, since our edition, at least in the present passage, does not differ much from them, let us consider that what has been said on theirs has been said on this also.

After such great evils it is said of them that they will lick the ground like serpents that drag the earth, walking on their belly and eating earth all the days of their life. And doing the works of the flesh, that is, earthly works, and dragging with them, up to the day of the vengeance and visitation of the Lord, not dust, not small traces of earth, but the whole ground. And when they have done this, and have come to the judgment of God, and have been shut in and troubled, they will be troubled and shut in for as long as the earth which they had dragged like serpents remains in them. But when that has failed, they will be astonished and will marvel, not at the Lord their God — for they will not yet deserve that he be called the Lord their God —, but at the Lord our God. And suddenly there is an ἀποστροφὴ (a turning of address) to Christ, and it is said to him: And they shall be in fear of you. For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.

Wherefore let us not listen to him when we are in any of the troubles of this world, be it bodily pain, or the loss of our children, or of other necessaries, let us not listen to his words, Where is the Lord thy God? It is under severe pain that his temptations are to be feared, it is then that he seeks to turn the sick soul astray.

Wherefore the soul which has not listened to his allurements, seeing afterwards the wonderful works of God, seeing herself in heaven, and the devil creeping upon the earth, will congratulate herself saying, Who is a God like unto Thee, that pardoneth iniquity and passeth by transgression?

For what was it Jesus' detractors said? "No man can forgive sins, but God alone." Inasmuch then as they themselves laid down this definition, they themselves introduced the rule, they themselves declared the law. He then proceeded to entangle them by means of their own words. "You have confessed," he says in effect, "that forgiveness of sins is an attribute of God alone; my equality therefore is unquestionable." And it is not these men only who declare this but also the prophet Micah, who said, "Who is a God like you?" and then indicating his special attribute he adds, "pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression."

Moreover, what follows, For those who are left of his inheritance, he did not hold his anger as a testimony, has this sense: if he spared the nations, which would not believe his law, and would not impute their iniquities to those who were left over and left remaining of the people, nor brought his anger as a testimony of their just punishment, what will he do with his own flock, which feeds in the midst of Carmel, and in Bashan, and in Gilead? For he is one who wills mercy, and returning he will have mercy on us; and our heavy sins, and the iniquities that sit upon the talent of lead, he himself will carry, and will sink in the sea, and will not let them appear.

I too will say at the end of the volume, sealing the labor of my little work with an invocation of the Lord: God, who is like you? Take away the iniquity of your servant; pass over the sin of the remnant of my soul; do not send your fury upon me, nor rebuke me in your anger, since you are merciful, and your mercies are many. Return, and have mercy on me; hurl down my iniquities, and cast them into the depth of the sea, so that the saltiness and bitterness of vices may perish in a false region. Give the truth that you promised to your friend Jacob, and the mercy that you promised to your friend Abraham, and free my soul from the persecutors of your prophets, Ahab and Jezebel, as you swore to my fathers in the days of old, saying: As I live, says the Lord. I do not wish the death of the sinner, only that he turn back and live, and elsewhere: As soon as you have turned and groaned, you will be saved. Then my enemy will see, and will be covered with confusion, she who now says to me: Where is the Lord your God? I will see your vengeance on her, and she will be like the mud of the streets, and will be trodden down, so that she may no longer build Egyptian cities out of mud and straw.

Who is a God like you? You who take away iniquity, and pass over the sin of the remnant of your inheritance. He will not send his fury any more, because he is one who wills mercy. He will return and have mercy on us; he will put away our iniquities, and will cast all our sins into the depth of the sea. You will give truth in Jacob, mercy to Abraham, which you swore to our fathers from the days of old. LXX: Who, O God, is like you? Taking away iniquities, and passing over injustices for those who are left of your inheritance? He did not hold his anger as a testimony, because he is one who wills mercies. He will return, and will have mercy on us, he will sink our sins; and all our sins shall be cast into the depth of the sea. He will give truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham, as you swore to our fathers according to the former days. The prophet, understanding that the multitude of the nations was troubled in its enclosure for this reason, that it might be astonished and fear God, and that the Lord rages for this reason, that he may take away sins and give salvation, praises the Lord and marvels, and says: Who is a God like you? Taking away iniquities, and passing over injustices, so that, just as the destroyer in Egypt passed over the people of Israel and did not lay it waste — and was it not from this passing-over that the phasa, that is, the pascha, received its name? — so you may spare the nations, in no way imputing to them their iniquities.

Moreover, where we translated, He will not send his fury any more, for "any more" Symmachus rendered "forever", Theodotion "to the end", the Seventy and the Fifth Edition "as a testimony", for which laed is set in the Hebrew; and it can be understood as "any more" as well as "forever" and "testimony".

We ought therefore to strip ourselves and give to him who is naked. One has God, another has him not at all—that contrary power, namely. And just as it is written that "we should cast our sins into the depth of the sea", so we ought to throw off from ourselves our vices and sins and cast them upon him who was for us the cause of them. "And he who has food", he says, "let him do likewise". He who has food, let him give to him who has none, so that he may bestow upon him not only clothing, but also that which he may eat.

"The Lord sits enthroned over the flood." A flood is an overflow of water that causes all lying below it to disappear. It cleanses all that was previously filthy. Therefore he calls the grace of baptism a flood, so that the soul, being washed well of its sins and rid of the old person, is suitable henceforth as a dwelling place of God in the Spirit. Further, what is said in the twenty-first psalm agrees with this. For after he has said, "I have acknowledged my sin, and my injustice I have not concealed," and also, "For this shall every one that is holy pray to you," he then said, "And yet in a flood of many waters, they shall not come near him." Indeed, sin shall not come near to one who received baptism for the remission of his transgressions through water and the Spirit. Something akin to this is found in the prophecy of Micah: "Because he delights in mercy, he will turn again and have mercy on us. He will put away our iniquities and will cast them into the bottom of the sea."

He will turn again and have compassion upon us; he will tread our iniquities under foot, and all our sins shall be cast into the depths of the sea. He will perform the truth to Jacob and the mercy to Abraham, as he hath sworn unto our fathers from the days of old.

He will give truth to Jacob, and mercy to Abraham, so that to the people that is a supplanter, and new, and always set in wrestling, he may render his truth in Christ, and to the multitude of the nations — for Abraham is called the father of many nations — he may grant mercy, as he swore to those who were the fathers of our faith according to the days of old, that out of the whole multitude of men he would save some in truth, others in mercy.
